10:45 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Trump leads attendees in pledge, says they'll 'go to hell' if they don't vote Terry Collins During his closing midterm convention remarks, President Donald Trump told attendees to take a pledge to vote Republican on Election Day. "You know what happens when you don’t vote, right? You go to hell," Trump said Thursday. "And I don't want that to happen to you, so please go and vote." The president concluded his speech in under 30 minutes, after the more than 90-minute marathon address he gave on Wednesday.

10:35 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Vance cheered with chants of '48' during rowdy convention address Francesca Chambers Vice President JD Vance had a high bar to clear in his convention speech, and attendees indicated in their reactions that he delivered. After a string of salty comments that included calling his boss the "toughest SOB in American politics" and telling a flag-waving protester, “If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there, I'll buy you the plane ticket," the vice president was cheered by MAGA voters and met with loud applause. "Ladies, I'd like to know what you had to drink," he told an especially rowdy group of women, "cause I'll take two of them when I'm done." Attendees responded by shouting "48" at Vance, who'd become the 48th president of the United States were he to run and win the 2028 presidential election, eliciting a grin from the sitting VP and a chuckle. "We've got to take care of business this November, then we'll worry about what comes next," Vance told them.

10:33 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Trump closes out the convention with music showcase Kinsey Crowley President Donald Trump promised to keep his remarks brief on night two. Shortly after taking the stage, he said, "I'm getting a little bit tired of politics now," though he touted his administration's policies on immigration, taxes and more. He said instead he would stand on stage while opera singer Christopher Macchio performs "Nessun Dorma," "America the Beautiful" and "All I Ask of You," from the musical "The Phantom of the Opera." The program also teased a balloon drop set to the songs, "YMCA" and "Pinball Wizard."

10:07 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Vance revisits spat with El-Sayed Kinsey Crowley and Melina Khan Vice President JD Vance during his keynote address revisited a public spat with Michigan's Democratic Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed. In August, El-Sayed responded to a clip on X of Vance referencing his late grandfather as he spoke about the Democratic candidate. El-Sayed responded to the clip by writing, "So do we think JD is taking Usha (Vance) with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…" Vance addressed El-Sayed at an Aug. 31 rally, saying, "keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth." The vice president again at the midterm convention mentioned his grandfather while recalling a visit to his hometown. "Abdul looks at him, sees the color of his skin, sees his background, and decides that he could never have loved my wife," Vance said. "This is who the Democrats are now." El-Sayed is in a tight race against Republican Mike Rogers, who spoke earlier in the evening. Rogers and multiple other speakers have sharply criticized El-Sayed's policies throughout the event.

10:03 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Usha said 'hell no' to convention, VP says Francesca Chambers Second lady Usha Vance wasn't in Dallas for a simple reason, her husband said at the convention: In July, she gave birth to their fourth child, Alec. "You should have been there when the organizers of the midterm RNC asked my wife, who had a two-week-old baby, and three other kids that are very young, if she would come to Dallas, Texas, to introduce her husband," Vice President JD Vance said. "She said, 'Hell no, I've got four kids to take care of,'" he added. "But she sends her love, and I know she's watching at home." Vance used the personal anecdote as a windup to promoting Trump administration policies that he said are helping American families.

10:02 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Vance makes pitch to skeptical voters: 'Not asking anybody to agree on every single policy' Zac Anderson Vice President JD Vance sought to appeal to voters who might have qualms with some of the Trump administration's policies in his speech, calling the alternative worse. "Look, I'm not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration," Vance told the crowd. "What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals, and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months." President Donald Trump's low approval rating is presenting a challenge for Republicans. With Democrats eager to make the election a referendum on Trump, much of the GOP convention has focused on setting up a contrast with Democrats by accusing the party of being too extreme.

9:50 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Protester waving flag kicked out of convention Zac Anderson Vice President JD Vance was interrupted by a protester he said was waving a Mexican flag. The man was quickly kicked out of the convention with a parting shot from the vice president that received a huge applause from the crowd. "If you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there and I'll buy you the plane ticket," Vance said as the crowd erupted with chants of "USA, USA." Vance continued: "We just discovered the symbol of the far left: An idiot waving... a Mexican flag at a protest when he should be waving the flag of the United States of America."

9:40 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Vance says convention a 'joyful' and 'somber' occasion as he honors Kirk Francesca Chambers Vice President JD Vance told attendees that the convention speech was both a "joyful occasion" and a "somber one" as he reflected on the anniversary of his close friend Charlie Kirk's assassination one year ago. Vance said that history will record that Kirk, the co-founder of Turning Point USA, was "a great man." Addressing his comments to Kirk's widow, Erika, and their two children, he added: "But those of us who loved your dad we knew him as something even better than a great man, he was a good man." Erika Kirk was in the arena on the first night of the Republican midterm convention, sitting with Vance and other Republican brass when President Donald Trump delivered his keynote address. Turning Point held its own event on Thursday evening at Utah Valley University, the college campus where Charlie Kirk was speaking when he was killed. Vance called into Kirk's namesake radio show earlier in the day. He hosted the program last September in the aftermath of the conservative activist's death.

9:00 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update RFK Jr. explains switch to Republicans Michael Loria Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the scion of one of the most famous Democratic political dynasties, said his switch to the Republican Party was largely a protest against Biden administration pandemic safety measures. "During Covid I watched the Democratic Party turn against every one of its essential values," said Kennedy. "My father nor my uncle would recognize the Democratic Party of today." Kennedy’s father was U.S. Sen. Robert F. Kennedy. His uncle was President John F. Kennedy. Both were assassinated, and the two are considered icons of liberalism. RFK Jr. argued that his family would have opposed mask mandates, school and church closures and supported people opposed to vaccines. He said his family’s values found a "new home" in the Republican Party. Still, many of the efforts he criticized took place under the Trump administration in 2020, and experts say the measures saved American lives during the pandemic.

8:47 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update What time does Donald Trump speak tonight? Kinsey Crowley Although President Donald Trump gave his keynote address already, he said he would come back on Thursday for closing remarks. Trump is scheduled to speak after Vice President JD Vance's keynote address. The program says Trump will start his appearace at 9:37 p.m. ET, but as of 8:35 p.m. ET, the program was about 25 minutes behind schedule. "I'm gonna close it out," Trump said during his initial remarks. "But I'm not doing a big deal like this because I don't have to say the same stuff twice. I gave you a lot of material." Trump spoke for about 1 hour and 45 minutes on night one of the convention.

8:29 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update 'Trumpalooza' drew 2.5 million viewers, Fox says Phillip M. Bailey President Donald Trump's midterm convention, which competed with the NFL regular season kickoff, didn't provide Fox News with a noticeable ratings boom, according to the network. The event, dubbed "Trumpalooza" by supporters, averaged about 2.5 million viewers during the first day, Fox News told USA TODAY in a Sept. 10 email. That's about the same amount who watch each night during conservative commentator Sean Hannity's program at 9 p.m. ET, which rakes in roughly 2.6 million viewers on average. The number of people who tuned in during the convention, which Trump and his allies hope will boost turnout this fall, peaked at about 2.8 million viewers around 9:45 p.m. ET during the president's speech. Many had questioned how well the GOP event would do in terms of ratings given that it aired during the same time as a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks on NBC.

8:26 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Cruz on support for Trump dividend: 'It depends how it's structured' Francesca Chambers Sen. Ted. Cruz, R-Texas, said in an interview with Fox News host Jesse Watters that he'd support President Donald Trump's proposed $5,000 dividend – if it were limited to working Americans and came in the form of a tax refund. "It depends how it's structured," Cruz said. "I would like to see it structured as a tax refund." Republicans should be doing everything they can to encourage people to work, he said. "I could easily see something like that passing."

8:21 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Emotional tribute marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 Terry Collins "Never forget" was a constant theme as the convention came to a pause during an emotional tribute to remember the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks in New York City. Tunnel to Towers Foundation CEO Frank Siller said in a video that he remembers the unity America displayed after the 9/11 tragedy that killed nearly 3,000 people. Siller started the nonprofit to assist fallen firefighters and their families after his brother, New York City firefighter Stephen Siller, died while in the World Trade Center's South Tower. "In our shock and grief, we all came together as one people, determined to help each other overcome and rebuild. We put aside our differences and became one American family," Frank Siller said. "We shouldn't wait for another tragedy to have that feeling again. Never forget." Following another video that showed the tragedy and aftermath of Sept. 11, a procession of first responders, families, and loved ones of fallen victims took the convention stage, accompanied by a performance of "Ave Maria" as the victims' names were displayed on a screen above them.

7:58 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Swing district Republican on Trump: We 'don't always agree' Zac Anderson A convention full of plaudits for President Donald Trump took a brief detour when New York Rep. Mike Lawler addressed the crowd. He's running in one of the most competitive districts in the country, one that he noted has more Democrats than Republicans. Some swing district Republicans, such as Maine Sen. Susan Collins and Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan, chose to skip a convention that risks tying them more closely to Trump. Others decided to show up and praise Trump as they work to fire up Republican voters in an election that could hinge on turnout. Lawler was somewhere between, attending the convention but gently distancing himself from Trump. He said his speech was for “common sense Democrats and independents… who are deeply concerned about the rise of socialism and extremism on the left.” “They aren’t exactly sold on Republicans either,” Lawler said. “I get it. I understand where you’re coming from. The truth is that the president and I don’t always agree, and that’s OK.” “After all, we’re both New Yorkers,” he added. “We argue. We tell each other what we think, and I know this might be hard to believe but there’s even some profanity.”

7:54 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Trump says Democratic control of Congress may not be that dire Francesca Chambers Even as he campaigned for Republicans in Texas at the midterm convention, President Donald Trump downplayed how damaging a Democratic takeover of Congress would be for his legacy. He told Fox News host Laura Ingraham in an interview that he'd use his remaining two years in office to block most of the opposing party's agenda, if that were to happen, and said Democratic control of Congress may not be that dire. Asked if it was just as important to help Republicans keep control of the House and Senate as his own election to office was, Trump began by saying: "It's never as important. Look, I'm campaigning for other people." "When you say my legacy, I'll be a block. I'll end up being blocker. I'll block all their bad stuff for two years. It won't be the same, but I'll be a blocker," Trump said. Trump suggested that he'd even be able to make some deals with Democrats, saying, "They're going to want some stuff." "So it's not as dire, maybe it is as dire," Trump assessed.

7:32 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Trump denies $5,000 dividend is MAGA socialism Francesca Chambers President Donald Trump denied that the $5,000 dividends he's promising to send Americans if Republicans win the House and Senate this fall are a form of socialism during a Fox News interview that aired Thursday evening. "You know what it is? It's real entrepreneurship, that's really what it is," Trump said. "It's not communism. It's actually good entrepreneurship." The promise of payment if his party wins is being panned by Democrats and even some conservatives, who argue that the proposal is a blatant bribe and would face obstacles in Congress. Appearing on "The Ingraham Angle" on Fox News, Trump also argued that he may not need congressional approval because the United States is taking in so much money through the investments like the one his administration made in Intel.

7:25 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Cruz and Johnson criticize Democrats ahead of midterm vote

7:18 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Charlie Kirk remembered in moving tribute at GOP convention Terry Collins Conservative activist and Turning Point USA Founder Charlie Kirk, who was assassinated a year ago today, was honored at the GOP midterm convention. Turning Point vice president Lucas Miles told Republican attendees that the best way to remember Kirk is to "pick up the mic" and carry on his message. Kirk was fatally shot while speaking at an outdoor campus event in Utah. "A voice can be silenced, but the truth cannot," Miles said, as chants of "Charlie, Charlie, Charlie," could be heard from the convention crowd. "A man can be taken from his post, but if he spent his life awakening courage in other men, his absence may accomplish the very things his enemies intended to prevent."

6:53 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Dems hold 11-point lead over Republicans in generic ballot poll Kinsey Crowley More voters want Democrats to win control of the U.S. House than Republicans by an 11-point margin, according to a Quinnipiac University poll published Thursday. Asked if the election were held today, 49% of respondents said they would want the Democratic Party to win, versus 38% who said they would want the Republican Party to win, and 13% did not offer an opinion. The margin is slightly wider compared to a July 29 poll, when 48% wanted the Democrats to win and 41% wanted the Republicans to win. Still, both parties have low approval ratings overall. Just 21% approve of how the Democrats are handling their job in Congress compared to 70% who disapprove. And 26% of voters approve of Republicans' job in Congress compared to 67% who disapprove. The poll was conducted Sept. 3-6 among 970 self-identified registered voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.9 percentage points.

5:54 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update These candidates speaking tonight are facing close races Kinsey Crowley President Donald Trump pushed for the midterm convention to help give Republicans their best chance at winning in the midterm elections. But not every Republican has opted to travel to the convention, nor is every Republican speaking at the convention facing a close election. The Cook Political Report is a nonpartisan, independent forecaster that rates races from "solid Democrat" to "solid Republican," with a handful it calls "toss-ups" in the middle. USA TODAY has gathered the "toss-up" Senate and House races, their candidates and locations as of Sept. 9 in a watch guide to help you understand the convention. The candidates in "toss-up" races who are listed on night two of the program include: Mike Rogers, candidate for U.S. Senate (Michigan)

Rep. Ryan Mackenzie(Pennsylvania)

Derek Merrin (Ohio)

Eric Flores (Texas)

Rep. Mike Lawler (New York)

5:25 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Talarico was GOP's top target on night 1; He's hitting back in media blitz Terry Collins While Texas state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, is in the crosshairs during the Republican Party's midterm convention, he's picking his spots to fire back. During an upcoming interview on MS NOW Thursday, Talarico agreed when asked whether President Donald Trump's promise that every adult U.S. citizen would get a $5,000 check if Republicans maintained their majorities in Congress is a bribe. Talarico questioned why Trump, who has called him "Talafreako," is waiting until after the election, when people are "sick and tired" of politicians "ignoring and grandstanding" on the affordability crisis, instead of finding solutions to lower costs. "This just feels like an election year stunt. And people in Texas are drowning. People in Texas are struggling to survive in this economy. They need real action, bipartisan action," said Talarico, who is in a tight race against the GOP Senate nominee, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "They don't need promises for after Election Day, especially when you already have the power to do it now if you truly care about affordability," Talarico added.

4:50 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Trump's $5K payout plan faces a maze of obstacles among Republicans in Congress Zachary Schermele WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump's pledge to give $5,000 to all adult U.S. citizens if Republicans keep control of Congress this November faces a maze of formidable obstacles on Capitol Hill – including from members of his own party. Regardless of the fact that Trump's other, similar promises haven't materialized – not to mention the legal questions surrounding his latest election-related proposal, which Democrats have chalked up to a "bribe" – there's no clear legislative path forward for approving or reshuffling what would ultimately amount to more than $1 trillion. Several budget hawks and conservative economists are already balking at the idea – a bad sign when just a few Republicans in either chamber can, until the voting margins change, tank pretty much any measure. "Frankly I’m insulted by the notion that my vote this November could be bought for 5k," Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, wrote on X, "not to mention the inflation this would cause." Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, appeared to chime in, too, saying in response to a post defending the proposed dividends that government "dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms." Read the full story

4:16 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Trump floats $5,000 checks 'if the Republicans win'. Is that a bribe? Christopher Cann, Jeanine Santucci and Aysha Bagchi WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump made the extraordinary pledge to give every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, sparking immediate backlash from Democrats who likened the offer to a bribe. “If the Republicans win, you win with us and you get $5,000,” Trump said Sept. 9, during a first-of-its-kind GOP midterm convention in Dallas. “It will be called the Trump Dividend.” Some Democrats quickly called out the promise. Rep. Dan Goldman, D-New York, called the pledge “corrupt and blatantly illegal.” Rep. Jamie Raskin, of Maryland, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, called the proposal a “political bribe” that would add $1.3 trillion to the “wreckage of this fantastically reckless and dysfunctional presidency.” USA TODAY spoke with several experts who were skeptical that the pledge was illegal, although there are many unresolved problems with the idea. Read the full story

3:50 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Midterm convention night 2 kicks off soon. How to watch: Kinsey Crowley The Republican midterm convention continues into night two on Thursday, Sept. 10, starting at 4 p.m. ET. USA TODAY reporters have been on the ground in Dallas, Texas, watching the event and bringing updates from the scene. You can also tune into the speeches live on USA TODAY's YouTube channel: The program will also be available on C-SPAN, which announced that it will provide the only complete, uninterrupted television coverage of the midterm convention. The outlet said coverage will be available on its website, television and radio stations, and on C-SPAN’s YouTube channel. Tune in here on Thursday, Sept. 10. Learn more about what other TV networks plan to cover the event, here.

2:58 pm ET September 10, 2026 Share this update Lining up for a picture with the MAGA Boyz Zac Anderson Dressed in red, white and blue shorts and knee socks, with MAGA hats, blue blazers, Converse high-top shoes and red shirts depicting President Donald Trump with glowing red eyes, the MAGA Boyz stood out at the cavernous Hilton Anatole as people milled about the hotel waiting to attend the second day of the convention. The group, which does canvassing for GOP candidates, formed after the assassination attempt on Trump at a 2024 rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. Devin Dashnaw, 34, of Plattsburgh, New York, said members of the MAGA Boyz were in the front row of the rally. A video one of them recorded of the shooting went viral, he said, and they decided to quit their jobs and "focus on helping Trump win the election that year." "We do whatever we can to further the Trump agenda and help this administration," Dashnaw said. Their Trump fandom has become a canvassing business, and their colorful clothes are a calling card. search_result.title: Beshear slams Trump as 'briber in chief' over $5,000 payment promise
search_result.text:
Updated Sept. 10, 2026, 5:28 p.m. ET

Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is hitting back at President Donald Trump’s proposed $5,000 dividends, calling the president “briber in chief.”

On Sept. 9, Trump made headlines during a Republican midterm convention with his promise to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans continued to hold the House and Senate after the midterm election, a proposal that carries a $1 trillion price tag and would likely require congressional approval.

During a press conference at the Democratic Governors Association's annual conference in Louisville, Beshear said it's "not legal to offer people money for their vote. But if we know one thing about Donald Trump, it's he's never paid a bill he's owed, whether it's in the private sector or as president. Where are those $2,000 rebates he promised all Americans? They absolutely never materialized.”

Trump's latest promise echoes others he's made in the past, including proposing $2,000 tariff dividends, which never came to fruition.

During the press conference, governors from across the country criticized the president's policies on tariffs, Medicaid and deteriorating relations with Canada. They were also quick to hit back on the president's efforts to bolster Republican voting ahead of the midterms.

Alongside Beshear, who currently chairs the association, Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly, Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson and Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer were in attendance, sharing how federal policies have impacted their states. Walz, who ran against Trump and Vice President JD Vance as part of the Democratic presidential ticket with Kamala Harris in 2024, said the president is “hell bent” on interfering with the upcoming elections.

“They're not out there knocking doors,” Walz said. “They're not out there telling you how they're going to lower prices. They're trying to figure out how to keep all those excited people from voting. It won't work.”

Keep up with our coverage: Sign up for our weekly politics newsletter.

Much of the governors’ concerns revolved around the federal government's tariffs and trade agreements with Canada, which have soured in Trump’s second term. In retaliation for the U.S. imposing 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, Canada has unveiled $20 billion in "dollar for dollar" tariffs, something the Democratic governors warned could severely impact industry and agriculture within their states.

For both Walz and Ferguson, whose states share borders with Canada, the impacts of economic tariffs have been devastating. But more than that, the loss of the relationship is isolating the U.S. from its closest trading partner and ally, Walz said.

“But this is so deeply cultural and so personal and so damaging,” Walz said. “And when you hear Prime Minister (Mark) Carney say, ‘We just have to recognize the United States we thought was there is no longer here and is gone,' and they're looking towards the European Union now, it is absolutely catastrophic globally.”

Reach Keely Doll at kdoll@courier-journal.com. Reach The Courier Journal's politics team at cjpolitics@courier-journal.com.

"We'll call it the Trump dividend." He added that Americans would only be able to spend the money in the United States. "We don't want you to be going to Canada to spend the money," he said. The president's "patience is running out," White House officials said in July when asked about the Senate not passing the SAVE America Act. Thune has resisted Trump's call to eliminate the filibuster and pass the controversial proposals, which would require proof of citizenship to vote and prohibit universal mail-in voting. search_result.text:
Updated Aug. 18, 2025, 2:45 p.m. ET

August is full of celestial events, and this week marks a milestone for the 4.503 billion-year-old planet known as Mercury.

Being such a small planet that lies close to the sun, Mercury can be difficult to see. That’ll change on Aug. 19, when planet-gazers on Earth can look up and see Mercury at its greatest distance from the sun, according to Time and Date.

This period where it is farthest from the sun, called the greatest elongation, happens twice every 116 days or so (or about every four months), reported Time and Date.

Elongation is essentially how far apart the sun and a planet appear when we look at them in the sky, the Pierce College Science Dome in western Washington shared on social media.

Because the planet appears farthest from the sun, the sun’s glare doesn’t impede our ability to see the planet as much, the college said.

More on greatest elongation and why it happens so often

According to Pierce College, there are multiple types of greatest elongations, including:

Greatest eastern elongation (also known as greatest elongation east): The planet is most visible in the evening just after sunset.

Greatest western elongation (also known as greatest elongation west): The planet is most visible in the morning just before sunrise.

The one space enthusiasts will see on Aug. 19 is the greatest elongation west, best visible in the morning, according to Time and Date. The next greatest elongation east will occur on Oct. 29, making Mercury most visible in the evening, Time and Date said.

According to Pierce College, Mercury reaches its greatest elongation six or seven times a year. Other planets such as Venus reach greatest elongation only twice per year, the college said. This is because Mercury orbits closer to the sun, and it doesn’t take as much time for the planet to make an entire orbit around the sun.

How can I see Mercury at its greatest elongation?

The best time to see Mercury during its greatest elongation is about 30 minutes before sunrise, according to EarthSky. It’s best to look in the direction of the sunrise as the sky gets lighter.

According to Time and Date, those wanting to see Mercury should not point their binoculars or a telescope in the direction of the sun.

“It can cause permanent eye damage," the website warns.

Saleen Martin is a reporter on USA TODAY's NOW team. She is from Norfolk, Virginia – the 757. Email her at sdmartin@usatoday.com.

search_result.title: Within a year, Voyager 1 spacecraft will be 1 light-day from Earth
search_result.text:
Updated Nov. 25, 2025, 4:40 a.m. ET

It takes a beam of light a single day to travel 16.1 billion miles, a distance known as a light-day. It'll take Voyager 1, the American spacecraft moving at 10.6 miles per second, more than 49 years to do the same.

Voyager 1, which launched in 1977 and explored Jupiter, Saturn and points beyond, will reach a light-day milestone in November 2026 when it becomes the first craft to travel 16.1 billion miles from Earth.

Distances in space are so vast, astronomers use the speed of light, 186,282 miles per second, to measure them. A light-day is the 16.1 billion miles traveled by light waves and radio signals in 24 hours. A light-year is nearly 6 trillion miles.

By comparison, our solar system is relatively small, averaging about 3.7 billion miles from our sun to Pluto.

Where is Voyager 1 right now?

Can't see our graphics? Click here to reload the page.

Voyager 1 rocketed into space aboard a Titan IIIE-Centaur from Launch Complex 41 at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977.

In flybys, the spacecraft extensively photographed Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980. It discovered volcanic activity on Io, a moon of Jupiter, and three new moons orbiting Saturn. It also found intricate structures in the ice shapes of Saturn’s rings.

Voyager 1 left our solar system in August 2012 but remains within the sun’s gravitational field. Since entering interstellar space, the craft has been studying plasma waves, cosmic rays and magnetic fields in the heliosphere, the immense bubble of solar wind around the solar system.

Though the spacecraft is the farthest human-made object from Earth, it's not the only space probe that's billions of miles away.

Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11, launched to study Jupiter and Saturn in 1972 and 1973, respectively, are no longer transmitting.

What is a light-year, a light-day, and an AU?

Light-year: 5.9 trillion miles

5.9 trillion miles Light-day: 16.1 billion miles

16.1 billion miles AU (astronomical unit): 93 million miles

There are about 63,241 AUs in one light-year.

How much longer will Voyager 1 last?

Engineers were able to fix an onboard computer glitch that rendered unreadable the science and engineering data Voyager 1 sent to Earth, The problem started on Nov. 14, 2023.

Engineers from NASA and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory discovered a single computer chip inside the spacecraft’s Flight Data Subsystem – which collects science and engineering information and transmits it – had malfunctioned.

The chip could not be repaired. Instead, engineers moved software code from the chip into a different part of the subsystem's memory system. That allowed data to be transmitted clearly.

Voyager 1's distance makes the craft difficult to control. A radio signal takes one day to send and another day for a response to be received. The time lag makes troubleshooting very slow and forces engineers to rely on autonomous systems and redundant hardware.

Voyager 1 is slowly losing power

The spacecraft is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. The RTGs are mounted on a boom and use plutonium-238 oxide that slowly decays and produces heat. The RTGs convert the heat to electricity.

Voyager 1 doesn’t use much power. At launch, the three RTGs combined produced about 470 watts at 30 volts of electricity, the equivalent of four or five 100-watt incandescent light bulbs.

The craft is down to about 230 watts now, the power of two 100-watt bulbs.

NASA has been shutting down systems on both Voyager craft to conserve power to allow them to continue data transmissions past 2030. Once they lose all electrical power, the Voyagers will keep traveling deeper into space for billions of years.

What is the Golden Record aboard Voyager?

Both Voyager spacecraft carry what's called the Golden Record, a 12-inch gold-plated copper disk that contains sounds and 115 analog images selected to represent life on Earth.

The record's aluminum cover contains a cartridge and a needle and has instructive diagrams that show how to play the record and decipher its information.

Carl Sagan of Cornell University chaired a NASA committee that chose the record's contents.

SOURCE USA TODAY Network reporting and research; Reuters; NASA; Jet Propulsion Laboratory; theskylive.com

Updated Aug. 27, 2026, 11:02 a.m. ET

For the second time this month, sky gazers in Iowa will have a chance to see an eclipse on Thursday, Aug. 27.

August's partial lunar eclipse, which is also called the "almost blood moon," will occur tonight, but only part of the country will be able to see the whole show.

The East Coast and parts of the Midwest will be able to see the entire eclipse, from start to finish, on the night of Thursday, Aug. 27, according to NASA. Other areas of the country, like the West Coast, will only be able to see the eclipse after it begins.

The eclipse will also be visible in western Europe, western Africa and the Southern Hemisphere, where all of South America will be able to see the entire eclipse.

Here's what to know about Thursday's partial eclipse and how to view it in Iowa.

What time does the lunar eclipse begin in Iowa?

The partial lunar eclipse will begin around 8:23 p.m. Thursday in the Des Moines area, according to Time and Date, but you might want to wait a while before looking up.

The best time to catch the partial lunar eclipse in Iowa, when the moon slips behind the maximum amount of Earth's shadow, will be at 11:12 p.m.

By 2 a.m. Friday, Aug. 28, the eclipse will be over in Iowa, according to Time and Date.

Will skies be clear in Iowa for the August 2026 lunar eclipse?

At 10 p.m. Thursday, much of Iowa is expected to have mostly clear skies, improving the chances of seeing the partial lunar eclipse. Cloud cover could reach 29% in parts of western Iowa.

Tips for seeing the partial lunar eclipse

The lunar eclipse is visible to the naked eye, and observers will not require any visual aids, such as telescopes or binoculars, to view it. Your phone can also be used to capture pictures of the eclipse.

Those who plan to stay up to watch the eclipse and want the optimal experience should do the following:

Check the weather and cloud cover in your area to ensure conditions are optimal for viewing the celestial events.

Find a dark location away from light pollution.

Give your eyes 20 to 30 minutes to adjust to the dark.

Avoid looking at phones or bright lights.

The moon rises in the east and sets in the west, so make sure you have an unobstructed view, clear of buildings or clouds, of the eastern and western horizons if you want to catch the moon rise and set.

search_result.text:
Editor’s Note: Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Tonight’s sturgeon supermoon could have you dancing in the moonlight – the type that only happens three to four times per year.

Named by the Native American Algonquin tribe after sturgeon fish that were more easily caught in the Great Lakes and other bodies of water during this time of year, the sturgeon moon ends 2022’s series of four supermoons, which began in May, according to The Old Farmer’s Almanac. After sunset, look toward the southeast to watch this supermoon rise. It will reach peak illumination at 9:36 p.m. ET Thursday.

“At certain times of the year, the moon is at its closest point to Earth and these are called supermoons,” said Mike Hankey, operations manager for the American Meteor Society, via email. “It’s just a natural point of the moon’s orbit. At each extreme, the moon is either a little bigger or a little bit smaller (at its furthest point), but it is not a huge difference.”

This nearest proximity is called the perigee, and it is only about 226,000 miles (363,300 kilometers) from Earth, according to NASA. That’s why a supermoon also appears slightly brighter than a regular full moon. The moon’s distance from Earth changes throughout the month since its orbit isn’t a perfect circle, according to The Old Farmer’s Almanac.

If you take a cool photo of the supermoon, you could share it on social media with the hashtag #NASAMoonSnap – the phrase NASA is using to track moon-inspired content leading up to the late-summer launch of Artemis I, the first test flight of the rocket and spacecraft that will send future astronauts to the moon, according to NASA’s Tumblr. The agency has shared a guide for photographing the moon, and will share some users’ content on its social media platforms during the launch broadcast.

The sturgeon moon will steal the spotlight of the Perseid meteor shower peaking Thursday through Saturday.

“Bright moon phases are bad for meteor showers as they wash out the dimmer meteors,” Hankey said. “A full or almost full moon dominates one part of the sky, making that part undesirable for observing meteors. The full moon also lasts the entire night, leaving no hours of complete darkness, which is preferred.”

The Perseid meteor shower lasts from July 14 to September 1, and this year’s barely visible peak will happen at 11 p.m. ET on Friday (3:00 a.m. UTC Saturday), according to EarthSky. In previous years, the Perseids have been a highly anticipated shower in the Northern Hemisphere, where it’s usually more visible. But that’s only when the moon isn’t in a phase dominating the sky.

This year, the Perseids – which strengthen in number from late evening to early dawn – were more visible in early August when the moon appeared smaller and dimmer. In previous years, they were most visible in nearly moon-free skies.

The shower’s fragments come from comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, which takes 133 years to orbit the sun just once, according to NASA. The comet last entered the inner solar system in 1992.

The sturgeon supermoon lights up the night sky 6 photos The supermoon — also called the sturgeon moon — rises as a jetliner approaches John F. Kennedy International airport on August 11 in New York City. Bebeto Matthews/AP The sturgeon supermoon lights up the night sky The supermoon — also called the sturgeon moon — rises as a jetliner approaches John F. Kennedy International airport on August 11 in New York City. Bebeto Matthews/AP The full moon is shown behind the Washington Monument on August 11 in Washington, DC. The sturgeon moon is the fourth and final supermoon of 2022. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images The sturgeon full moon rises next to Istanbul's Çamlica Mosque on August 11. Chris McGrath/Getty Images A paddle boarder watches the rising sturgeon moon off Swanpool Beach on August 11 in Falmouth, England. Hugh R Hastings/Getty Images The full moon sets behind apartment houses in the outskirts of Frankfurt, Germany, early Friday, August 12. Michael Probst/AP A moon gazer takes a selfie as the supermoon sets in the early morning hours above Kosice, Slovakia, on August 12. Robert Nemeti/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images Prev Next The sturgeon supermoon lights up the night sky

Remaining space events in 2022

Four more full moons will occur this year, according to The Old Farmer’s Almanac:

September 10: Harvest moon

October 9: Hunter’s moon

November 8: Beaver moon

December 7: Cold moon

Other Native American tribes have different names for the full moons, such as the Cheyenne tribe’s “drying grass moon” for the one happening in September, and the Arapaho tribe’s “popping trees” for the full moon occurring in December.

Catch the peak of these upcoming meteor shower events later this year, according to EarthSky’s 2022 meteor shower guide:

Draconids: October 8-9

Orionids: October 20-21

South Taurids: November 5

North Taurids: November 12

Leonids: November 17-18

Geminids: December 13-14

Ursids: December 22-23

And there will be one more total lunar eclipse and a partial solar eclipse in 2022, according to The Old Farmer’s Almanac. The partial solar eclipse on October 25 will be visible to people in Greenland, Iceland, Europe, Northeast Africa, the Middle East, West Asia, India and western China.

The total lunar eclipse on November 8 can be seen in Asia, Australia, the Pacific, South America and North America between 3:01 a.m. ET and 8:58 a.m. ET. But for people in Eastern North America, the moon will be setting during that time.

Wear proper eclipse glasses to safely view solar eclipses, as the sun’s light can damage the eye.

July 19, 2026 Updated July 20, 2026, 11:43 a.m. ET

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket is scheduled to launch from California on Monday, July 20.

The rocket will carry 24 Starlink satellites into low-Earth orbit.

Viewers can watch a livestream of the launch on SpaceX's website.

Update: The launch was scrubbed and is now being targeted for no earlier than 7 a.m. PT Tuesday, July 21. For more information, visit here.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket will soon get off the ground in California on what will be the 50th launch of 2026 in the state.

The two-stage rocket, the most active in the world, has been the vehicle to launch on nearly every single spaceflight this year from the Vandenberg Space Force Base. And unsurprisingly, the 50th launch will also be yet another Starlink satellite delivery mission – by far the most common at the launch site.

Want to make sure you don't miss the big mission? While plenty of places near Vandenberg reliably attract spectators, you can also tune into SpaceX's livestream.

Here's everything to know about the latest SpaceX mission, and how to watch a webcast of the Falcon 9 launching in Santa Barbara County.

Is there a rocket launch today? Next liftoff from California

SpaceX is working toward a Monday, July 20, launch from Southern California, with a four-hour launch window opening at 7 a.m. PT. The launch will take place from the Vandenberg Space Force Base in Santa Barbara County.

A Federal Aviation Administration operations plan advisory suggests a backup opportunity is available the next day if the launch were to be postponed.

What is launching from Vandenberg? Falcon 9 to deploy Starlink satellites

SpaceX will launch its famous two-stage 230-foot Falcon 9 rocket, one of the world's most active, to deliver 24 Starlink satellites into low-Earth orbit, an altitude nearer Earth's atmosphere where they're able to circle the planet quickly.

How to watch SpaceX launch livestream

Californians, of course, have plenty of opportunities to see a rocket in person both near the launch site as it lifts off, and farther away as it soars overhead.

But SpaceX also provides a live webcast of its missions for those who prefer to watch from home or for those viewing the launch locally and looking for updates in real-time.

As with most SpaceX missions, the launch will be available to stream on the company's website and its new X TV mobile app, beginning about five minutes before liftoff. SpaceX may also provide updates on social media site X.

Photos of SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket in California, US

Does Elon Musk own SpaceX? What to know about rocket company

SpaceX is the commercial spaceflight company that billionaire Elon Musk, the world's richest man, founded in 2002 and leads as the CEO.

SpaceX is headquartered at Starbase in South Texas near the U.S.-Mexico border. The site, which is where SpaceX has been conducting routine flight tests of its 400-foot megarocket known as Starship, was recently voted by residents to become its own city.

As a major government contractor, SpaceX serves as the launch service provider for a variety of government missions both civil and military.

For the Department of Defense, SpaceX's Falcon 9 helps launch classified satellites and other payloads into space. And for NASA, Falcon 9 most often helps propel astronauts to the International Space Station on SpaceX's Dragon crew capsule – the only U.S vehicle capable of carrying NASA astronauts to orbit.

What is Starlink?

Starlink is SpaceX's internet satellite business.

With more than 10,000 satellites in its growing orbital constellation, Starlink has become a lucrative part of Musk's business empire, serving millions of customers around the world.

Eric Lagatta is the Space Connect reporter for the USA TODAY Network. Reach him at elagatta@usatodayco.com

AP

Updated Oct. 15, 2012, 8:31 p.m. ET

Cole will get his 99th international cap

England plays Poland on Tuesday in a World Cup qualifier

The Chelsea left back caused a stir by tweeting controversial comments about the English FA

LONDON (AP) — After another off-field misdemeanor, Ashley Cole will hope to do his talking in Poland on the pitch on Tuesday and nudge England closer to the World Cup.

The defender didn't feature in Friday's 5-0 rout of Marino, with coach Roy Hodgson insisting that wasn't punishment for a vulgar Twitter outburst against the Football Association.

Whether he was dropped or rested, Cole now can't reach a century of England appearances in Warsaw — and he's facing increasing competition for the spot at left back.

Leighton Baines has started all four England games since the European Championship, although Cole was injured for the August and September matches.

"Ashley has deserved every one of his 98 caps and hopefully he will reach the 100 mark because he deserves it," Baines said. "I don't think I will be denying him that. It will happen. Ashley is a top player and I'm sure he will get to the milestone."

On his 99th international showing Tuesday, Cole is likely to be the most experienced member of the defense as England copes without center back John Terry, who quit international football before the FA punished him for racially abusing an opponent.

It was after reading criticism of his role defending Terry in the case that Cole turned to Twitter to criticize the FA.

"Getting involved in what he has been involved in at the moment has been unfortunate," former England defender Martin Keown said. "He has been misunderstood to a large extent. For all that, what you cannot argue with his success on the football field because Ashley is a phenomenal player.

"He keeps putting in the performances year after year ... if he had a point to prove he has proved it."

England will hope to gain more than just a point in Poland.

Although the easier games against Moldova and San Marino have been won so far in qualifying on the road to Brazil in 2014, Roy Hodgson's side was held at home to Ukraine last month.

And while England holds a three-point lead in Group H, Montenegro and Poland have each played a game less.

Hodgson will need Wayne Rooney to pick up where he left off against San Marino on Friday when he scored twice to rise to fifth in the England scoring leaderboard on 31.

The Manchester United striker will relinquish the captain's armband to midfielder Steven Gerrard, who returns from suspension.

"At the moment I am seeing the best of Wayne Rooney," Hodgson said. "Maybe in the earlier games he could play for me he wasn't at that level. Now I have to hope now he stays at his best and that he stays fit and healthy and continues to do what he is doing for Manchester United at the moment, which means he'll do it for us as well."

While the ball rarely even entered England's half against San Marino on Friday, Poland struggled in a friendly against South Africa.

Waldemar Fornalik's side won 1-0 in just his second game in charge courtesy of Marcin Komorowski's debut goal.

Captain Jakub Blaszczykowski will be missing with an ankle injury, while Przemyslaw Tyton is set to remain in goal in placed of the sidelined Wojciech Sczcesny.

But Poland's main goal threat is fit: Robert Lewandowski, who has scored four times this season for Borussia Dortmund but failed to beat Manchester City and England goalkeeper Joe Hart in their Champions League encounter.

"Lewandowski played well in that game," Rooney said. "He had the runners either side of him and they counter attacked very well. That is something we have to be aware of because we know Poland are a good counter attacking team. We will have to deal with that.

"But, as long as Joe plays well, I'll be happy. He is a fantastic keeper and he is certainly the best to come out of England for a long time."

search_result.text:
Aug. 23, 2025 Updated Sept. 3, 2025, 3:55 p.m. ET

Land a dream job at 29. Buy your first home at 30. Earn six figures by 35.

Realistic or not, those are the ages Americans ascribe to some of life’s financial milestones, according to a new survey from Empower, the retirement services provider.

Empower asked roughly 1,000 Americans to set target ages for six life milestones: retirement saving, landing a dream job, earning six figures, buying a home, becoming debt-free, and retiring.

The findings, published in August, are tinged with regret. Nearly half of respondents said they wish they had started saving sooner. Nearly a quarter said they felt behind in reaching money milestones. Many respondents said there’s no set timeline for reaching big financial goals.

And some dates on the timeline seem more dream than reality. Buy a first home at 30? These days, the average first-time buyer is pushing 40.

Do you work for a great organization? Nominate it as one of America's Top Workplaces

USA TODAY asked several experts to comment on the six milestones in the survey. Here’s what they said.

Age to start saving for retirement: 27

If you start saving for retirement any time in your 20s, retirement planners say, you’re doing great.

“I didn’t personally start until I was 29,” said Andrew Herzog, a certified financial planner in Plano, Texas. “Now, that is absolutely one of my regrets.”

In a perfect world, however, 27 might be a tad late to start saving for retirement.

“Especially if you’re entering the workforce at 16, 17, 18, you’re depriving yourself of 10 years of saving,” said Catherine Collinson, CEO of the Transamerica Center for Retirement Studies.

The good news, Collinson said, is that younger Americans are saving for retirement early. Transamerica research shows the typical Gen Z worker started saving at 20. Millennials started at 26, Gen X at 30, boomers at 35.

And why wait till 20?

“I’m a big believer in trying to get your kids set up for retirement when they’re teenagers,” said Catherine Valega, a certified financial planner in Winchester, Massachusetts.

Age to land your dream job: 29

The average American changes jobs a dozen times between ages 18 and 56, according to a Labor Department report on boomer workers.

That data point suggests that most of us don’t find a dream job by 29: If we did, presumably, we’d stay put.

“Dream jobs don’t expire at 29,” said Randy Bruns, a certified financial planner in Naperville, Illinois.

“Putting a deadline on something so personal risks discouraging the very people who are still on their way,” he said. “Imagine someone telling Colonel Sanders he should’ve had it all figured out by age 29. He didn't start serving fried chicken until he was 40.”

Age to buy your first home: 30

First-time homebuyers are getting older. The average first-time buyer was 38 in 2024. That’s the highest age the National Association of Realtors has ever recorded.

Home prices have spiked dramatically since 2020. Mortgage rates have risen, as well, making homes less affordable to first-time buyers.

“It’s still possible to buy your first home by 30, but it’s much harder now than it was for previous generations,” said Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin.

Buying a home by 30 used to be a realistic goal. The average first-time buyer was 30 in 2010 and 33 in 2020, according to the Realtors association.

Today, however, many young buyers are priced out.

“Some are making it work by getting help from family, opting for a condo instead of a house, or choosing to live in a neighborhood that’s affordable on their income,” Fairweather said. “So, it’s still possible, but it takes a lot of planning and often support from friends or family.”

Age to earn six figures: 35

Many Americans will never earn a six-figure income. The average full-time American worker earned about $1,200 a week in the second quarter of 2025, or about $62,500 a year, according to federal data.

For some workers, a six-figure income is a realistic hope. People with doctoral or professional degrees earn more than $100,000 a year in median pay, according to a NerdWallet analysis. And income tends to rise with age, peaking around 50.

Even so, reaching a six-figure salary by your mid-30s “seems more aspirational than realistic for most jobs,” said Lonnie Golden, an economist at Penn State University's Abington campus.

Age to become debt-free: 41

There are different kinds of debt, and not all are bad.

A financial adviser might frown on a $10,000 credit card balance with a 20% interest rate. But a homeowner who nabbed a 3% mortgage in the low-interest years might still be bragging about it to the neighbors.

“Debt can serve a good purpose, depending on its use,” Herzog said. “If you can strategically use your debt, there’s no problem with carrying it.”

Financial planners typically urge consumers to work on reducing “bad” debt, especially credit card debt.

A mortgage, by contrast, can function as a massive piggy bank, with your equity rising every time you make a payment.

“Some people prioritize paying down debt over other goals for psychological reasons, and that’s fair – it doesn’t feel good to have a big number hanging over your head,” said Sam Taube, lead investing writer at NerdWallet. “Mathematically speaking, however, prioritizing debt over all else may not always be the optimal strategy.”

Age to retire: 58

Retirement plans can change over time. Younger Americans generally aspire to retire earlier. Older Americans plan to retire later. According to a 2025 Schwab survey, the average Gen Zer expects to retire at 62, while the average Gen Xer plans to wait until 66.

“The reality is, as people get older, they realize how much they need to save,” said Collinson of Transamerica.

By most measures, retirement experts said, 58 is a little early to pack it in.

“To retire at 58, you’d need millions of dollars in a brokerage account, or very low living expenses in retirement,” said Taube of NerdWallet. “Possibly both.”

Sept. 6, 2026, 5:53 p.m. ET

At least five people are dead and five others injured after an Amazon cargo plane overran a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, Sept. 6, according to Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz.

The Federal Aviation Administration and Amazon confirmed the plane came down striking multiple vehicles. The incident forced the closure of one of the nation's busiest airports.

In a statement to USA TODAY, Miami International Airport confirmed that the plane overran the "diagonal runway and is disabled at the northwest end of the airport." All runways and taxiways are closed.

More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the scene. The fire department said the plane struck multiple vehicles and is "assessing patients," though it is unclear if any injuries have been reported.

A video of the crash obtained by NBC News Miami shows fire and a black cloud of smoke billowing from the aircraft. The FAA has issued a ground stop at the airport until at least 5:30 p.m. ET and said it is investigating the incident.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said travelers using Miami International Airport should expect delays and potential cancellations.

Air Flight 7598, an Amazon Air Boeing 767-300 jet, had departed San Juan, Puerto Rico, earlier in the day Sept. 6. "We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," Amazon said in a statement to USA TODAY. In January 2025, an American Airlines regional jet collided with an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Reagan Washington National Airport, killing all 67 people aboard the two aircraft. Sept. 7, 2026 Updated Sept. 9, 2026, 11:10 a.m. ET

An Amazon Prime Air cargo plane overran a runway while landing at Miami International Airport on Sept. 6 and struck two vehicles, killing five people and injuring five in a "devastating" accident, authorities said.

Amazon Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-300 freighter operated by Miami-based 21 Air LLC, arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, shortly before 2 p.m. ET when it overran the runway, National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy said at a news conference. The aircraft had two people on board.

The plane struck navigational equipment before hitting a van carrying seven workers from a contract cleaning company, then struck another vehicle traveling on a roadway outside the airport perimeter fence, Homendy said.

Five people were killed and five were injured, including three who were in critical condition as of Sept. 6, authorities said. Miami-Dade Fire Chief Ray Jadallah said at least two people had been trapped in vehicles hit by the aircraft, and the pilot and copilot had been trapped inside the plane.

More than 60 rescue units and about 200 emergency personnel responded to the crash. Emergency personnel battled a fuel leak from the plane hours after the accident, authorities said.

The NTSB launched an investigation and sent a team to the scene. Homendy said the crash path stretched about 1,300 feet beyond the paved runway and described the scene as "utter devastation."

Preliminary timeline of Amazon plane crash

Homendy said the aircraft landed at about 1:53 p.m. ET on Sept. 6 and overran the runway, striking navigational aids and equipment before hitting a 2012 Ford Econoline van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a contract cleaning company for airlines. Seven people were inside the van.

The plane then broke through a perimeter fence and hit a Toyota Corolla Cross traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue outside the airport before sliding into a grassy area and crashing through another fence near an area where Tesla Robotaxis were stationed, Homendy said.

Authorities said the deaths and injuries were limited to occupants of the two vehicles. The van was on airport property, and the SUV was outside the airport perimeter.

When firefighters arrived, the plane was engulfed in flames. They used a specialized foam to extinguish the fire and worked to rescue victims, authorities said in a statement.

Video of the accident obtained by NBC News Miami showed a cloud of black smoke billowing from the aircraft. Photos from Reuters showed the aircraft with its nose on the ground and tail tilted up. The right side of the plane had what appeared to be scorch marks.

NTSB investigation underway as airport operations recover

Homendy said investigators were still gathering and verifying information and had not yet gained full access to the aircraft because of recovery operations and fuel removal.

Investigators recovered the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder on Sept. 7, Homendy said. The devices were being taken to NTSB headquarters for analysis.

The Amazon plane was making its third flight of the day, the NTSB said. The aircraft had flown from Cincinnati to Miami, then from Miami to San Juan before returning to Miami.

The 32-year-old aircraft carried passengers for several airlines from 1994 to 2015, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.

The NTSB said the investigation will examine numerous factors, including the operational relationship between Amazon and 21 Air. Federal authorities also noted that determining the cause of the accident will take time.

USA TODAY reached out to the flight's operator, 21 Air, for comment.

Flights at Miami International Airport canceled, delayed

The crash came during the Labor Day travel rush at one of the nation’s busiest airports. As of 9 a.m. ET Sept. 7, airport spokesperson Greg Chin said the aircraft had not yet been relocated. Two of the airport’s four runways remain closed, Chin said.

The airport temporarily halted flight operations after the crash. Travel disruptions continued into Sept. 7, and inbound flights were delayed by more than five hours on average, according to FlightAware.

At least 89 flights were canceled, and more than 300 others were delayed at the airport Sept. 7, data from FlightAware showed. The airport advised travelers to check with their airline for schedule changes.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said travelers using Miami International Airport should expect delays and possible cancellations.

"We're working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened," Amazon told USA TODAY in a statement. "Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved."

Sept. 9, 2026 Updated Sept. 10, 2026, 7:51 a.m. ET

Federal investigators said Sept. 9 that one of the pilots of the Amazon Prime Air cargo plane that overran a runway at Miami International Airport repeatedly commented about the aircraft's excessive speed during the final one minute and 42 seconds of the cockpit voice recording.

In an investigative update, the National Transportation Safety Board said there was not a consistent verbal response to the remarks about speed and that the aircraft's system announced "Too low, terrain" several times before the plane touched down. The agency did not identify which pilot made the comments.

The latest findings come as the wife of one of the victims killed in the Sept. 6 crash filed a wrongful death lawsuit alleging the accident was caused by multiple failures involving the two pilots aboard, aircraft operators and others connected to the flight.

Investigators have not determined the cause of the crash, which killed five people and injured five others after Amazon Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-33A operated by 21 Air LLC, overshot the runway and struck two vehicles. Preliminary findings from the NTSB have pointed to questions about the aircraft’s speed as it approached the runway and the crew’s handling of the landing.

Fifteen seconds before the cockpit voice recording ended, one of the pilots called for aborting the landing and "throttles were increased to a value consistent with go-around thrust," according to the NTSB. But four seconds later the throttles were pulled back to idle, and the recorder caught sounds similar to the plane departing the paved runway surface.

The agency previously said there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed to help slow the aircraft.

Lawsuit alleges 'series of failures' in Amazon cargo plane crash

The wrongful death lawsuit, filed Sept. 9 in Miami-Dade County Circuit Court by Yaraisi Santiso Morejon, seeks damages over the death of her husband, 53-year-old Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, who was driving a van when the Boeing 767 overran the runway.

The complaint names Amazon.com Inc., Amazon Air Cargo, Miami-based cargo carrier 21 Air LLC and the two pilots as defendants. The suit alleges pilot error, inadequate training and the deployment of a 32-year-old aircraft whose systems are under investigation.

"We allege that this was not a freak accident, but a foreseeable and preventable disaster caused by negligence," Morgan & Morgan attorney Mike Morgan said in a statement. "What we've already uncovered points to a series of failures by the people flying the plane, the companies that put it in the air and the systems that were supposed to prevent this exact kind of tragedy."

21 Air has said it is cooperating with the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration and local authorities. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel previously said the company would fully cooperate with investigators and continue coordinating with 21 Air, which operated the flight.

Lawsuit alleges series of failures in Amazon cargo plane crash

According to the complaint, the Boeing 767 overran the runway shortly before 2 p.m. Sept. 6 and traveled about 1,300 feet beyond the pavement before crashing into two vehicles. Five people were killed, all occupants of a van owned by a contract cleaning company for airlines and another vehicle, authorities previously said.

"The crash killed five innocent people and seriously injured five others, three critically," the lawsuit states. "The victims were airport workers and a motorist on a public road, people who had every reason to believe they were safe. They were not."

The van was a 2012 Ford Econoline owned by Professional Ocean Service Corp., which was carrying seven employees, according to authorities. It was inside airport property at the time of the crash. The second vehicle struck was a Toyota Corolla Cross traveling outside the airport's perimeter fence.

The suit alleges the pilots of the aircraft continued an unstable approach in tailwind conditions, landed too far down the runway, and failed to initiate a go-around before the aircraft overran the runway.

The complaint also alleges Amazon and 21 Air failed to adequately train and supervise pilots and allowed unsafe operational practices. It further claims the companies involved placed into service a 32-year-old aircraft whose braking, thrust reverser and spoiler systems are among components being examined by investigators.

The NTSB is continuing its investigation into the incident, which occurred after the cargo jet arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day. The aircraft, operated by 21 Air on behalf of Amazon Prime Air, had earlier flown from Cincinnati to Miami and from Miami to San Juan before the crash.

The aircraft departed with a takeoff weight of 252,182 pounds and was expected to land at 231,236 pounds, according to Homendy. The plane's cargo weighed 32,222 pounds and consisted primarily of contact lenses.

Investigators said no hazardous materials were aboard.

Sept. 8, 2026 Updated Sept. 9, 2026, 11:13 a.m. ET

Federal investigators said Sept. 8 that flight recorder data from an Amazon Prime Air cargo plane suggests the pilots may have considered aborting the landing moments before the aircraft crashed at Miami International Airport, killing five people on the ground.

The crash happened shortly before 2 p.m. on Sept. 6. The Amazon Air Flight 7598, a Boeing 767-33A operated by 21 Air LLC, arrived from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and overran the runway, leaving a crash path of 1,300 feet beyond the paved runway in a scene described as "utter devastation" by National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy.

Five people were killed, all occupants of two vehicles, a van owned by a contract cleaning company for airlines and another vehicle, according to Homendy. Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said five others were taken to hospitals, including two pilots on board the plane who were treated and have since been released.

During a news conference Sept. 8, NTSB investigator Chihoon Shin said flight data showed the aircraft's nose landing gear and right main landing gear touched down about 30 seconds before the recording ended. The left main landing gear touched down about 19 seconds before the end of the recording.

Then a few seconds later, the brakes were released and the throttles were increased to "values consistent with go-around thrust," according to Shin. He added that there was no indication in the recorded data that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.

"When we analyze the full list of parameters, we'll have a better idea of the aircraft performance during this landing. Was it normal? Was it not? And what was working and what was not?" Shin said.

Homendy said investigators plan to interview both pilots on Sept. 9 before releasing a summary of the cockpit voice recorder, which captured more than two hours of audio. The flight data recorder contained about 55 hours of data and recorded more than 400 aircraft parameters.

"We want to hear their account of the accident before we release a readout of the cockpit voice recorder," Homendy said during the news conference.

The NTSB also released information on the pilots' experience. Earlier on Sept. 8, local authorities identified the pilots as First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37, and Capt. Joseph Carol, 55.
