search_result.title: 'Jurassic Games: Extinction' to premiere at deadCenter Film Fest OKC
search_result.text:
Updated June 13, 2025, 10:17 a.m. ET

Ryan Bellgardt's "The Jurassic Games: Extinction" makes its world premiere at the 25th Annual deadCenter Film Festival.

The sequel utilizes Boiling Point Media's LED Virtual Production Studio for filming.

"The Jurassic Games: Extinction" will be available digitally, on demand, Blu-Ray, and DVD following the festival.

While his actors take turns straddling a contraption that resembles a motorcycle chassis crossed with a mechanical bull, writer-director Ryan Bellgardt grabs his bullhorn.

"Here we go — and wind," the Edmond filmmaker cues a crew member, who obliges by switching on a leaf blower and pointing it at actor Bronsonn Taylor. "Good job, Bronsonn, just keep riding. ... Give me a 'whoa!' –— like a big one. You probably just almost got stepped on by a giant dinosaur that just barely missed you."

As the apparatus underneath Taylor bucks and rocks, it's the backdrop of towering trees that seems to be zipping across the high-definition LED screens surrounding the performer inside Boiling Point Media's LED Virtual Production Studio in Oklahoma City.

"It's like the 'Speed Racer' bullpen riding day," jokes Boiling Point owner and operator Emily Taylor, standing back from the bank of computer monitors where Bellgardt and his team are watching the scene unfold.

She nods and smiles in agreement when Bellgardt decides, "Yeah, that looks cool. All right, cut. Great job, Bronsonn."

As the next actor gets ready to take his turn on what will appear as a racing speeder in Bellgardt's science fiction sequel "The Jurassic Games: Extinction," Shawnee-based actor Adam Hampton strolls out of the makeup room, his face carefully smeared with dirt and soot for when the filmmaker digitally sets the forest on fire later that same April 2024 evening.

"I've been very fortunate to have been a part of these films. ... It's awesome to be busy doing what I love," said Hampton, who is reprising his role as Tucker in Bellgardt's second "Jurassic Games" movie.

The sequel to his 2018 homegrown cult-favorite film "The Jurassic Games," Bellgardt's "Jurassic Games: Extinction" will make its world premiere at the 25th Annual deadCenter Film Festival, which continues through Sunday, June 15, at various Oklahoma City venues.

When can film fans see the made-in-Oklahoma sequel 'Jurassic Games: Extinction?'

Oklahoma's largest and only Oscar-qualifying film festival, deadCenter 2025 boasts an eclectic lineup of 200 independent features and short films — including 25 world premieres — representing a roster of nearly 40 Sooner State filmmakers, as well as additional moviemakers from across the globe.

A past winner of the festival's Oklahoma Film Icon Award, Bellgardt said he is thrilled to return to deadCenter with the world premiere of "The Jurassic Games: Extinction." His first near-future film about a virtual-reality game show that pits death-row inmates against fearsome dinosaurs also debuted at deadCenter, where it received the Special Jury Narrative Feature award.

"Years ago before I started making movies, I went to deadCenter as a fan and watched all the amazing films showcased there. It sparked a dream in me to make movies of my own," Bellgardt said.

"The early movies I made were crazy sci-fi action stories, and I was fortunate to screen them at deadCenter. As the years went by, I moved away from that genre, but now I've gone back to my roots with this movie. And it's awesome to come full circle by having its world premiere at the festival that started it all."

As part of deadCenter 2025, "The Jurassic Games: Extinction" will screen at 5:30 p.m. Friday, June 13, and 4:30 p.m. Saturday, June 14, at Harkins Bricktown 16.

"It picks up right where the first one left off ... when they're prepping for the next season of 'The Jurassic Games,'" Bellgardt said. "Before they can get the death-row inmates into the game, there's a glitch in the system. So, they send a team of expert game testers. ... When they get in there, the games actually start, and they have to play. And it's a matter of life and death."

Filmed entirely inside Boiling Point's virtual production studio using live virtual camera trackers, in-camera special effects and large LED walls that form what's known as a "volume," "The Jurassic Games" sequel next will debut on digital and on demand June 24.

Distributed by Jackrabbit Media, an independent production and global sales company, "The Jurassic Games: Extinction" also will be released on Blu-Ray and DVD on July 22.

During a break in filming at a spring 2024 set visit, Bellgardt chatted with The Oklahoman about playing another round of "The Jurassic Games" with Boiling Point's more advanced moviemaking technology:

Q: Why did you want to revisit the world of 'The Jurassic Games?'

The real answer is because we think enough people liked the first one that maybe they'd want to watch this one. (laughs). The first movie has a little bit of a following; there's a lot of people all around that like that first one. A while back, I just went on Twitter asking, 'Hey, I might make another one. Would anybody be interested?' And I got a lot of response from that. ... So, the idea started with 'OK, I can go back to a world that's already been established out there.'

But then once I started diving into it, you know, it's been seven or eight years since we did that first movie ... and I got to see Katie Burgess play Joy again. I got to see Adam Hampton play Tucker again. And we get to expand on these characters and give them more depth and more story — and that was just really exciting. It was really cool to see them bring those characters back to life.

Q: But the filmmaking technology that you use has changed a lot since you made the first 'Jurassic Games,' right?

Yeah, big time. ... One thing that I liked about the first movie is that we went all over the state of Oklahoma to a bunch of cool locations: We have the desert and the forest and just all kinds of crazy stuff. We built a big set for our control room. But over the last few years, especially during COVID, I got into virtual production, which includes using video game engines to create virtual worlds and then shooting them against either green screen or LED walls. And I've gotten really into that.

So, this movie, we thought, was the perfect opportunity to take our experience with that tech and kind of push it to the limits of what we can do with it. We partnered up with Jon Shryock and his fabrication company, and they've provided lots of practical props and things for the set. But they've also provided their robotic camera arm. Combining the robotic camera arm with the LED wall volume is allowing us to do things that just are way beyond what we could have ever done before in creating incredibly cinematic shots or helping us do repeated movements for visual effects and things like that.

So, the tech has come so far in the past seven or eight years, to allow guys like us to just push our stories and our creativity even further.

Q: This is one of the first entirely virtual production feature films made in Oklahoma, so what are your thoughts on taking the lead?

We might be the first that are crazy enough to try it. It's really an ambitious project. And it's something that I thought was maybe kind of risky to try, because, as far as I know, no one around here has done a feature film completely on an LED wall volume (before).

We're not shooting anything anywhere else. It's all done here. So, everything from their living room to the jail to the control room, to the burning forest to the snow, all that stuff is done in a very small space. But the neat thing about the tech is that we can make it look like it's a whole new world, and I think that's the really exciting thing about it. So, hopefully, we can pull it off.

Q: What is something new that you got to create for the sequel?

One of the things that I like from the first movie was that it was kind of set inside of a video game that they played. So, for the second one, I wanted to lean into that.

So, there's power-ups, and people can change into dinosaurs or upgrade their weapons and things like that. So, we leaned into more of the video game thing.

25TH ANNUAL DEADCENTER FILM FESTIVAL

search_result.title: I guarded Ground Zero and served in Middle East. Then I saw a ...
search_result.text:
John Byrnes

Opinion contributor

Sept. 10, 2026, 6:04 a.m. ET

I remember running toward downtown Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, like it was yesterday.

I was in the National Guard then and studying at Hunter College when I saw the north tower of the World Trade Center get hit on TV. Without much thought, I ran down Lexington Avenue to my armory. I wasn't sure of anything except that I needed to be there.

My fellow Guardsmen, many of whom were native New Yorkers like me, reacted the same way, showing up throughout the morning without being called in.

I didn't watch what was happening in Pennsylvania or Washington, DC. I was experiencing what was happening to New York – watching police and firefighters headed toward danger, people fleeing as quickly as they could and, eventually, feeling the rumble of the towers collapsing.

As I stood guard at Ground Zero for the next two weeks, I was processing collective trauma and rage I still cannot put into words. America was at war, and I believed almost anything we did next was righteous and justified.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

In the years that followed, I deployed to Afghanistan and Iraq and was fully on board with what we were doing. More hawk than dove, I championed the wars and believed that we could eliminate the terror threat and give these nations democracy, and that all would be well.

We just had to keep going.

But over time, the mission became harder to explain, even to ourselves. What began as a mission to punish those responsible for Sept. 11 and prevent another attack became an effort to remake the Middle East in our own image. We were still getting shot at and blown up; we were just less sure of why.

As presidents waged war in the Middle East, Congress abdicated its duty

I came to recognize a pattern. Presidents warned Americans of danger, Congress increasingly ceded decisions about military action to the president, and soldiers were asked to pursue poorly defined objectives that were disconnected from an immediate threat to the United States.

Repeatedly, we seemed to assume that enough military force could produce the political outcome we wanted. President Donald Trump's war with Iran is the latest chapter in this story, but the problem is bigger than one president or one party. For 25 years, Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden continued the expanded use of American military power in the Middle East while Congress repeatedly avoided its own duty to decide when and why the country goes to war.

That has led me to a humbling conclusion. The certainty I felt after Sept. 11 – that military force was justified, and that enough of it could make us safer – was easier to sustain than the wars themselves. Our leaders kept asking the military to produce outcomes that military power alone could never deliver.

I blame presidents of both parties for stretching their authority, but I blame Congress more for letting them. The Constitution gives Congress responsibility to declare war. To someone who has been sent to war, that is not a procedural technicality.

A vote forces our elected representatives to take responsibility for the lives they are asking service members to risk, and for the objectives they are asking them to achieve. Yet Congress hasn’t voted to approve military action in the Middle East since 2002.

Lawmakers think they are avoiding accountability by not voting to authorize military action, but many are sealing their fate in the coming midterm elections. This newest war is wildly unpopular among Americans, and they are reminded of it every time they fill up their gas tanks. They cannot make the president pay for that in November, but they certainly can take frustration out on his party.

Congress can begin repairing our trust. Start with Iran.

I struggle with how to commemorate Sept. 11 every year. I want to honor the people we lost that day. But as the years have passed, I have found it impossible to think about Sept. 11 without also thinking about everything that followed. Thousands died in the post–Sept. 11 wars. Tens of thousands more post-Sept. 11 veterans have died by suicide.

Some service members who have died in the current conflict with Iran were not even born when the attacks of Sept. 11 set this era of American warfare in motion.

After enough years, the dead become statistics and wars become abstractions. But the people who bear their consequences are someone's sons, daughters, mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters and friends. Real consequences for Congress' inaction.

I served in Iraq. An arms race could be catastrophic. | Opinion

There is another cost to this pattern: Americans will stop believing their government when it tells them another military threat requires their sacrifice. What happens when a threat to our national security comes along that truly does?

Congress can begin repairing that trust now. It should debate and vote on the war with Iran, define what American forces are being asked to accomplish, and decide whether those objectives justify asking Americans to kill and die for them. If Congress believes they do, its members should be willing to say so publicly and put their names behind that decision.

If Congress decides this war is necessary, so be it. America's military will always answer the call. I know that because on Sept. 11, before anyone called me, I ran to my armory.

Twenty-five years later, I still believe in that willingness to serve. What I no longer believe is that the people we send to war should have to wonder why they are there, what they are expected to accomplish, or whether the elected representatives who sent them were willing to take responsibility for the decision.

The men and women who answer America's call deserve at least that much.

John Byrnes is strategic director at Concerned Veterans for America and a veteran of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. He served at Ground Zero following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

search_result.title: 'The towers are gone!' Since 9/11, nothing has been the same.
search_result.text:
Opinion Forum

USA TODAY

Sept. 7, 2026, 6:02 a.m. ET

As we near the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, you've no doubt seen more of the tributes, the horrifying tales recounting loss and survival, and the tender moments of unity that feel so fleeting now.

As we revisit that history and remember the nearly 3,000 people who died in the attacks that day, we wanted to hear from you, our readers, on how you view one of the nation's most foundational shared memories. So we asked you what you experienced that day, what you remember from that moment of both unimaginable loss and of coming together as Americans, and how you see the legacy of that dark day now, with 25 years of hindsight and history.

See a collection of your responses below. For more opportunities to weigh in with your takes on the news, visit usatoday.com/forum, leave us a voicemail at (202) 655-3923 or drop us a note at forum@usatoday.com.

Where were you on 9/11? What do you remember? Tell us. | Opinion Forum

'The towers are gone!'

I was on a Long Island Rail Road train to Penn Station when we first heard of a plane crashing into the first tower of the World Trade Center. We thought it was a small plane, but I could see the smoke rising from the building. I entered the subway, but it stopped running, so I walked to Chinatown. Everyone was walking the other way, and cars were playing the news on the radio.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

I called my wife, who said, "The towers are gone!" I thought I would have heard it, but I checked the web, and it was true. I walked back to Penn Station and waited for hours until they released one train back home. When I got home, I couldn't turn off the TV, watching the news coverage.

Nothing was the same after. More security at airports, the military at public locations. What should have been done differently is that we should have been more diligent and direct in going after the people behind the attack. We ended up in a war for more years than we should have, and people are paying the price even now.

Having worked downtown, my office was closed for a week, but I went back and had to pass the rubble every day, walking to work. I'll never forget two things: 1) the posters everywhere of missing people and 2) the smell. In 2009, I was diagnosed with cancer, which I thankfully beat.

I think we do a wonderful job of remembering that day every year by taking a moment of silence for each plane and for when the buildings fell. We remember the victims by reading their names, so we never forget. The reflecting pools are beautiful reminders of the people and buildings. The 9/11 museum is a trove of history that everyone should see. Thanks to the Victim Compensation Fund, many first responders are able to get the treatment they need and the money they deserve for volunteering.

I'm not sure what justice looks like 25 years after 9/11. Too many have died, and there's nothing anyone can do to bring them back. What would justice look like?

This was the worst foreign attack on American soil in our history. This is a day no one should forget, but I think that 9/11 is to people who weren't born then as Pearl Harbor or the Vietnam War is to Generation X. We don't do enough to remember the day, just what's read in textbooks. Bring survivors and first responders to schools to tell their story.

— Craig Markowitz, New York

I felt helpless on 9/11. I found a way to help today.

I remember most the feeling of helplessness on 9/11.

Watching the TV coverage over and over, those fleeing Lower Manhattan, covered in dust. The loved ones holding up pictures and pleading for any information about those missing. Friends, family members, firefighters.

I knew there was nothing I could do to bring back those lost. Donating blood that wasn't needed. Donating supplies like flashlights, gloves, food for the rescue workers. It was a day of tragedy, but also a day of unity.

Since 2002, I have been part of the 9/11Day.org program, honoring those fallen with community service. Each year, I have been at the USS Intrepid packing shelf-stable meals for local New York City food banks.

This year, 50 locations are hosting events – planning to pack 18 million meals for food banks.

I will be in Miami, which is hosting for the first year. We can unite for good.

— Ellen Bowen, Florida

For a short time, we were all united as Americans

I was in Pompton Lakes, New Jersey, visiting my mom on Sept. 11, 2001. I had recently moved to St. Louis. We had planned on going the next day to the World Trade Center; my wife had never been there. That morning, my mom called the house from work and said the Trade Center was on fire and we probably couldn't go. So I turned on the TV, and saw the second plane hit. I knew at that point this was a terrorist attack.

I have pictures of the smoke coming up over Manhattan. It was one of the most dreadful days I have ever experienced.

I think a lot of Americans back then had a false sense of security that we were safe. 9/11 made us realize we were not. That day made most communities in the Northeast really come together since it was so close to home. When I got back to St. Louis, people were upset, but it was different. New York City was far away, and it didn't impact them as much. I still get sad thinking about that day, today.

As a first responder myself, we have been through our highs and lows. The people who died that day trying to rescue others were heroes of the highest order. Unfortunately, over the past 25 years, social media has brought the few bad officers into the spotlight and painted all of us with a broad brush. We dedicate our lives to helping others and don't ask for anything in return.

Sept. 11 was a horrible experience, but the country was briefly united. Right now, this country is so divided, and it seems it's MAGA vs. Democrats. Back on that awful day, we were just Americans. Grieving and comforting each other.

— Marc Beiner, Missouri

Sept. 11, 2001, started out as a lovely day

I worked in Midtown Manhattan at the time, and I distinctly remember, as I was walking from Grand Central station to my office, thinking just how lovely a day it was.

I'm at my desk settling in with my usual coffee, checking online for any news or baseball items of interest, when I notice that the internet is really slow for some reason. That's when someone comes in and tells us that a plane hit the World Trade Center. I putter about doing some work for a while, not even going to watch the TV that someone had set up in another room. I know that in the first few hours after every disaster or breaking news story, there's nothing but confusion and guessing – so I always wait a while before checking the news.

Around noon, we were told we could go home, because the office was closing and would be closed the next day. Things were open again on the 13th as we pretty much knew what had happened and needed to get on with things. I recall hearing an announcement on the subway: "Because of an incident at the World Trade Center ..."

Rather an understatement.

— Richard Solensky, New York

May we learn from our past and stay out of foreign wars

I dropped my husband off at Sacramento International Airport that morning and told him I wish he could be home for his 29th birthday that day. I returned home, and he called and said to turn on the TV. I saw a plane hit the Pentagon. His plane was grounded on the tarmac. I drove back to SMF to get him. Everyone leaving the plane got the news and was crying. It was surreal.

I was able to meet my husband at the gate on 9/11. Never again. I also became more skeptical of our world. Innocence was lost.

We need to honor our first responders and the pilots and flight attendants. I try to remind my children how life was before and after 9/11, and they're both well-versed in what happened.

What America needs now is to stay out of foreign wars. This is what got us into this trouble to begin with.

— Johanna Naughton, California

search_result.title: 'What happened at the Pentagon?' If we're not careful, 9/11 attacks ...
search_result.text:
Jacqueline Jules

Opinion contributor

Sept. 11, 2023 Updated Sept. 9, 2024, 9:41 p.m. ET

“The Pentagon is broken,” he said. “I saw the hole from my daddy’s car.”

The child was a preschooler in one of my library classes. He approached me after story time. I recall his little hands cupping my ear as if he were sharing a secret.

Like everyone in the Washington, D.C., area, this young child had a story to tell after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. One of my friends in Arlington, Virginia, was surprised by a vase falling from a bookshelf when the impact of the Pentagon crash jolted nearby houses. Others were frightened by the smoke and the sirens. Another family I knew was spared tragedy because the mother arrived late to work at the Pentagon that particular Tuesday morning. Many people were panicked by the lack of cell service as they tried to get through to loved ones and co-workers.

The Pentagon was broken. A gaping hole could be seen from the road. But it was repaired within a year. And in 2008, a beautiful memorial was erected on the grounds of the complex. The Sunday my husband and I visited, we got lost in one of the massive parking lots. A helpful security guard directed us.

When we finally arrived, we spent a thoughtful hour in silence walking among 184 cantilevered benches made of stainless steel with inlaid granite. On each bench, a name is inscribed. The ages of victims range from a 3-year-old aboard American Airlines Flight 77 with her family, to a 71-year-old Navy veteran also on the hijacked flight.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

In addition to the beauty of the 9/11 Pentagon Memorial, I must note that my husband and I were practically alone – so different from other memorials in the area generally packed with tourists. At the time, I appreciated the quiet, but in retrospect I wonder whether the absence of visitors that day reflects a larger truth about the collective memory of Sept. 11.

'Many people are surprised to hear that the Pentagon was ever a target'

The Pentagon sits across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C., in Arlington, Virginia. In a recent conversation with a group of Northern Virginia friends, I asked whether they had visited the 9/11 Pentagon Memorial. They responded that they didn’t even know a memorial existed there.

News coverage of the 9/11 terrorist attacks focused primarily on the carnage in New York City. Anniversary coverage does, too. Who doesn’t immediately recognize an image of the Twin Towers collapsing? Could the same be said for an uncaptioned picture of the damage done to the Pentagon?

Do Americans even remember that a jetliner also crashed into the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001?

A synopsis on the Arlington Public Library website for "9/11 Inside the Pentagon," a PBS documentary about the attack, notes that “many people are surprised to hear that the Pentagon was ever a target, let alone the loss of life that occurred there.”

Are kids learning enough about civics? If we want to make history, we must understand it first.

'What happened at the Pentagon?'

In 2008, I was a librarian at a public elementary school in Northern Virginia. After viewing a snippet of the televised dedication ceremony at the 9/11 Pentagon Memorial, a group of my students expressed sincere surprise. “What happened at the Pentagon?” they asked me.

If students in Virginia don’t know, what about students in Idaho or New Mexico?

We're still living with 9/11. Just like we're learning to live with COVID-19.

I will acknowledge that the Washington area did not experience the same death toll as New York City, where 2,753 lost their lives that Sept. 11. The Pentagon building still exists, unlike the demolished Twin Towers. But 9/11 was not just an attack on New York.

As the headquarters of the U.S. Department of Defense, the Pentagon is a symbol of American security. That symbol was shattered in 2001.

Monday marks the 22nd anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks. This year and in subsequent anniversaries, we should be cognizant of the 184 lives lost in Virginia and the 40 who died when terrorists crashed another jet in Pennsylvania. We should ask that this history be a part of the curriculum in all American schools.

Now, only a fraction of the 50 states require students to be educated on the events of Sept. 11, 2001. When a subject is not required, it is not given precious instructional time, particularly in schools that struggle with standardized test scores.

If we are not careful to teach the next generation, the 9/11 terrorist attacks will fade into a brief news story given coverage only on milestone anniversaries. Those who died 22 years ago deserve to be more than a footnote in American history.

Jacqueline Jules is a poet and author of more than 50 titles. In 2001, she was living in Arlington, Virginia, and working as a librarian. Her collection of narrative poems, "Smoke at the Pentagon: Poems to Remember," recalls the Northern Virginia experience of 9/11. Visit her online at www.jacquelinejules.com

search_result.title: He held the door for others on 9/11. His family never let it close.
search_result.text:
Sept. 11, 2026, 6:03 a.m. ET

Robert Fazio has had to piece together the last moments of his father, Ron, through conversations with those who had seen him in the south tower of the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.

He was in the Aon Corporation offices on the 99th floor when the plane struck the south tower. Although employees were told to return to work, he urged his coworkers to evacuate instead.

On the way out, his coworkers told the family that Ron Fazio held the door open for people as they descended the stairs to get out of the building.

In what would be his last moments, Ronald C. Fazio Sr. chose kindness.

“His instinct was to put others first, just like he always was, and how he lived his life,” Rob Fazio told me from his New Jersey home days before the anniversary.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

The family handed out flyers that described Ron’s height, weight and the scars on his chest and left leg. They asked whoever found him to feed him Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups. Despite this, the family buried an empty casket in New Jersey the following year.

“While we didn’t find him, we found his inspiration, which really became the cornerstone for everything my family and friends have done for the last 25 years,” Rob Fazio said.

A family mourns – and creates a way to help others

This year marks the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks that killed 2,977 people and impacted millions who watched it unfold. Ron Fazio's story, as told by his son, helped me better understand that day and the grief we have all lived with for two and a half decades.

At the time of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, Rob was in a psychology doctoral program at Virginia Commonwealth University. He changed his dissertation topic to focus on the emotional impacts of the day on grieving families.

It ultimately led him and his family to found Hold the Door for Others in his father’s memory the following year, a nonprofit dedicated to fostering growth through feelings of grief. He learned what works through both his studies and experience.

“When it was time to look for my dad, I could buck up and be like ‘Okay, we’re looking for my dad and my family friends,’” he told me. “And then, when it was time to cry hysterically and grieve and be like ‘Where’s my dad?’ I was able to do that, and I knew all of that was normal.”

How to explain 9/11 to kids? Start by not making this promise. | Opinion

How I learned what 'never forget' really means

I don’t remember where I was on Sept. 11, 2001. I was four years old and living in North Carolina. I don’t remember whether I went to preschool, saw anything on television or even sensed my parents' fear. I recently asked them about it. My dad, a banker, told me about the turmoil it wreaked on our financial system, while my mom said she had to choose between staying informed and shielding me from the tragedy unfolding on the news.

Now, as I approach my 30s and as a New York City resident, I have a clearer picture of what happened that day.

I know people who were affected. To learn more, I recently took a trip to the 9/11 Memorial & Museum. The One World Trade Center loomed over me as I walked past the tourists, yellow and blue hot dog carts and signs for luxury apartment buildings in the Financial District. As I passed by St. Paul’s Chapel, an Episcopalian church that became a place for recovery workers to gather in the aftermath, I saw banners put up by the city that said, “never forget.”

Most people in Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, were not alive when the attacks happened. For most of my generation, Sept. 11 is just another day. When we picture the New York City skyline, we don’t imagine the Twin Towers. We have forgotten, because there is no memory to retain. What I have learned is that for people who lost loved ones or were simply living in the tri-state area when the attacks happened, there is no forgetting.

“I don’t think, in American culture, we do grief enough justice,” Rob told me. “It impacts us more than we know. For some reason, we have this cultural norm of, it’s an adjustment period for three months, and then you’re fine, but no. It lives with you for the rest of your life.”

It surprises me that the Fazio family was able to start the nonprofit so quickly, in the midst of their pain. But it speaks to a throughline of our conversation: one of the many ways to grow in grief is to share what you're feeling with people in your life, whether it's sadness, anger, or moments of levity.

In fact, I was surprised to learn in my conversation with Rob that humor in tragedy helps us connect and is a healthy part of healing.

While Gen Z has the humor part down, I do think we struggle to remember a day we may not have been alive to see. That's why it's important to learn more about the day, experience the human condition at its most vulnerable, and listen to survivors' stories and what happened that day and in the period following the attacks. That's part of the reason New York City public schools recently set aside $1 million to educate students on the Sept. 11 attacks.

The 9/11 Memorial and Museum showed me the impact of Sept. 11, 2001

I knew from friends who had visited the museum that it was a somber place. I wasn’t prepared for how much it moved me.

As you walk into the start of the museum, you’re greeted by a hall of voices reacting to the day, while quotes and photos reflect on a series of screens. You reach an alcove overlooking the rest of the museum, featuring a map that shows exactly where you are in relation to the original buildings.

The main exhibit details, down to the minute, what happened that day, from the polls that opened that morning to the president’s return to Washington, DC, that night. There were floppy disks and burned papers from the rubble, which struck me – I guess I forgot that these were actual office buildings.

On a display of headlines from Sept. 12, I found the USA TODAY front page front and center – a picture of the Twin Towers aflame, with the headline “Act of War” summarizing the day. Our DC offices at the time were right by the Pentagon – multiple people in the newsroom reported seeing the explosion. In 2011, former USA TODAY writer Rick Hamson, who wrote the front-page story, said it was a “blessing, of sorts” to be able to cover the events. I understand the sentiment – it feels true, even now. To learn and write about it is the best I can do to express love to my fellow Americans, especially my fellow New Yorkers.

A photo of Ron Fazio is on the wall of the “in memoriam” section of the museum, alongside the images of 2,976 others who died that day, plus the six who died in the Feb. 26, 1993 bombing. His name is etched in bronze on the border of the 9/11 Memorial. He is remembered as an equal in death, alongside his coworkers and family friends, a piece of a larger story about a dark day in American history.

But my conversation with Rob showed me the man his father was, and the figure he remains even though he is no longer here. He is remembered through his son, who now helps others navigate grief. He is remembered every time his small grandchildren hold the door open for strangers. He is remembered, and that is how he lives on.

Remembering what happened in 9/11 will always be important

As I walked out of the museum and toward the memorial pools flowing toward an unknown center, I thought about how the country I live in changed that day, and how my life changed before I was old enough to understand.

I don’t know what to make of the world created by 9/11. I find myself stuck grappling with how the United States responded – the forever wars, the Islamophobia, the paranoia. I struggle with the fact that our country responded with vengeance. Perhaps I would feel different if I remembered the day.

Yet during my visit to the museum, I thought about the grief of it all, and how, in our conversation, Rob Fazio told me that the things that mediate the pain of grief have not changed for thousands of years.

“We went back to the core of human beings,” he told me. “Ok, there’s pain. If people share that pain, then the pain is less intense. If people aren’t afraid of you because of that pain, the pain has less power.”

The way we remember 9/11 is complicated. Grief is complicated. But as I saw at the memorial and museum, it's important that we remember the severity of the day and the lives lost.

Follow USA TODAY columnist Sara Pequeño on Bluesky: @sarapequeno.bsky.social

search_result.title: A nation marks 25 years since 9/11. 'We will always remember you'
search_result.text:
Updated Sept. 11, 2026, 5:00 p.m. ET

NEW YORK – A young girl climbed onto a stage here in Lower Manhattan and read the name of her late aunt and namesake, Maria Theresa Concepcion Santillan.

“I wish you could celebrate my birthday with me tomorrow," she said. "Please continue watching over us and know we all love and miss you.”

A moment later, a young boy standing beside her honored his grandfather and namesake, Andrew Ira Rosenblum.

“We will always remember you," he said. "We love you. God bless America.”

Both are among mourners who never met loved ones killed on 9/11, underscoring how much time has passed since the deadliest terrorist attack on American soil. Nearly a third of Americans were not alive that Tuesday.

Twenty-five years ago, 19 terrorists associated with al-Qaida hijacked commercial airplanes, crashing into the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers and the Pentagon. Passengers and crewmembers on a fourth plane fought back, forcing the terrorists – who were piloting the plane toward Washington, D.C. – to instead crash into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

In all, the attacks killed nearly 3,000 people that day, including more than 400 first responders, the single deadliest day for such emergency workers in American history, according to the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Many more have died from related health effects since.

Mourners observed the 25th anniversary in ceremonies across the nation on Sept. 11, 2026, including at the Pentagon and the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania and in Boston, where two of the fated flights originated. The ceremonies reflected a broad range of responses, from gratitude to grief to anger. They also illuminated the political polarization that grips America today.

In New York, four former U.S. presidents watched as first responders solemnly carried a huge U.S. flag on a stage at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum in Lower Manhattan. The renowned cellist Yo-Yo Ma performed as mourners read victims’ names. In the crowd, relatives held up photographs of their loved ones. Some lingered in front of the memorial pools, studying their relatives’ inscribed names and leaving behind flowers and miniature U.S. flags.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, attended the event, though he faced Islamophobic attacks and calls to skip the ceremony from conservative politicians. Standing steps away from him was former Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, who helped unify New Yorkers after the attacks before becoming embroiled in controversy years later. Giuliani previously said Mamdani’s presence would offend him.

The rhetoric was a sharp contrast with the efforts to unite the nation in 9/11’s aftermath. Amid rising Islamophobia in the days after the attacks, then-President George W. Bush visited the Islamic Center of Washington and declared “Islam is peace.”

Some mourners who spoke at the 25th anniversary event in New York condemned Saudi Arabia for allegedly supporting the hijackers. The Saudi government has consistently denied any involvement or foreknowledge of the attacks, saying in court that it remains a U.S. ally and is a sworn enemy of al-Qaida. The legal battle continues to this day, just blocks from Ground Zero.

"For 25 years, administration after administration, including leaders in front of us here today, chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families," said Terry Strada, an official with 9/11 Families United and the widow of Tom Strada, who was killed at the World Trade Center on 9/11.

Drawing applause, she thanked Vice President JD Vance for attending the ceremony, adding: “Please carry that message back – stand with the families, stand with the survivors, stand with Americans. As my husband Tom would have said, ‘That is always the right thing to do.’”

Barbara Pemberton, 74, of Williamsburg, Virginia, emphasized unity. She attended the ceremony in New York to show appreciation for responders and to honor her sister, Sue Sauer, who was in the World Trade Center for a work meeting on 9/11. On her right wrist, Pemberton wore a bracelet inscribed with Sauer’s name.

Pemberton, a retired educator, said she hoped younger Americans would spend time learning about 9/11 and how the country united in its aftermath.

“I wish we could go back to the day after 9/11 and see how patriotic people were then,” she said. “We are so divided now and it breaks my heart.”

'Great American courage'

As the sun rose, the U.S. 911th Technical Rescue Engineer Co. unfurled an enormous U.S. flag down the west side of the Pentagon, where 184 were killed after American Airlines Flight 77 struck the building. The tradition occurs every 9/11 anniversary, commemorating the first responders who hung a flag on the building 25 years ago.

The United States Marine Band performed “God Bless America.” Military officers read victims’ names as screens flanking them displayed their photos. The only other sound came from planes flying overhead.

Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, recalled how Pentagon staffers battled the smoke and fire and helped rescue others.

“Today is not just a story of loss; it is also a story of great American courage, selfless service – and those who’ve made the choice to carry those memories forward,” Caine said. “In the moment of greatest danger, Americans moved toward one another.”

Visitors were able to explore a corridor of the Pentagon near where the plane hit. The walls feature pictures of the disaster and cleanup along with children’s artwork commemorating victims.

Outside, President Donald Trump praised Americans for their resolve in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks. They responded, he said, to “wickedness. On days like 9/11, we learned what a country is truly made of.”

“Americans are made of a goodness and a spirit that can transcend any earthly force,” Trump said, “and that’s what we’re doing better than anyone else has ever been able to do it, because we are sustained by a supreme strength far more powerful than steel alone.”

Trump’s focus veered to America’s continuing war with Iran as he praised U.S. service members who are “working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror – the Islamic Republic of Iran – will never ever have a nuclear weapon.”

Hallowed ground in Boston

Teresa Mathai stood on the steps of the Massachusetts Statehouse, reading “We Remember Them,” a poem by Rabbi Sylvan Kamens and Rabbi Jack Riemer. Her husband, Joseph Mathai, died in the north tower of the World Trade Center. Their children, she said, are now married with children of their own.

“At the rising sun and at its going down, we remember them,” Mathai, of Arlington, Massachusetts, recited to the crowd of mourners.

The crowd echoed her: “We remember them.”

After Mathai finished the poem, Gov. Maura Healey and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu read the names of the 219 Massachusetts residents who were killed in the attacks.

“On this day, 25 years ago, our world was shattered in a single morning. We lost parents, grandparents, spouses, partners, siblings, children, friends,” Mathai said. “In those raw, painful autumn days of 2001, none of us knew how we would survive the weight of such sudden, devastating loss. Yet out of that unprecedented darkness, something profound emerged: unity.”

Mourners also gathered at Boston Logan International Airport, where American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175 departed before they were hijacked on 9/11. A memorial at the airport bears the names of the those who were on those planes. Archbishop of Boston Richard Henning prayed for them.

“We have in the Catholic tradition a ritual for blessing churches and cemeteries – hallowing the ground. But it strikes me that there's more than one way to make ground holy, and I feel so honored to be with you today,” Henning said. “And I feel very truly that we are standing right now on hallowed ground, holy ground.”

Flight 93

Davanna Feyrer was 3 on 9/11. She recalled watching Elmo on TV that day when "all of a sudden I saw a plane crash into a tower. I didn't understand." Now 28, she observed the 25th anniversary with her mother and father at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania. The memorial honors the 40 people who died when United Airlines Flight 93 crashed into a field here.

Feyrer’s family is from Butler, about two hours away. She has watched as the memorial has grown over the years.

"Something different happens to me every year. My favorite is the Tower of Voices,” she said, referring to a 93-foot monument featuring 40 windchimes. “A couple of years ago I took a really neat picture of it and made it my Facebook profile photo."

Her mother, Minnetta Bowman, said their family visits yearly because “it was just everyday people who stepped up to the plate and showed their support for each other and for our country.”

Deborah Grantham drove from Tennessee so she could attend the ceremony. Flight 93’s passengers, she said, "knew their plane was going to do something horrendous, and they decided to fight back. It just spoke to me."

Like others, she hopes the 25th anniversary will help reunite Americans.

“We all came together,” she said, “and I hope we come together again. I hope there's more reaching across the aisle – more being Americans, rather than thinking of individual wants and needs.”

Bailey Allen, Christopher Cann, Bart Jansen and Erin Mansfield contributed to this report.

search_result.title: 9/11: Heroes of Flight 93 gave their lives to save others - USA Today
search_result.text:
Tom Ridge

Opinion contributor

Sept. 10, 2021, 6:00 a.m. ET

Twenty years have passed since the terror attacks of Sept. 11. It’s a milestone to be sure. But no amount of time can fade my memories of that day.

What I remember most about 9/11 is stepping off the helicopter at Shanksville, Penn. – and being met by the brutal sound of silence. Emergency personnel searched the fields. Ambulances were at the ready. Rescue workers wanted someone to save.

But the passengers and crew of Flight 93 – 40 heroes strong – were the first, first responders on the scene.

They had already run toward the danger. They had already taken up the battle. And they were already in the arms of God.

USA TODAY's opinion newsletter: Get the best insights and analysis delivered to your inbox.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

A wonderful group called Friends of Flight 93 National Memorial has created a Heroes Award in their honor so their story is never forgotten. Could anything be more appropriate?

Above a Pennsylvania field, and the Pentagon’s stone and the once-towering World Trade Center, we lost nearly 3,000 souls from more than 80 nations. We lost them too terribly and too soon.

And yet, despite the weight of pain and anguish on our shoulders, we pulled together.

Do you remember? Some of you brought foil-covered plates of food to firefighters. Others held candlelight vigils in cities, large and small. Stores ran out of flags. Schools and communities raised money for grieving families. On the steps of the Capitol, members of Congress sang “God Bless America."

At our country’s worst moment, we survived on a steady diet of kindness, generosity and compassion. You may not find those words in any national security plan. But I can assure you – those concepts are just as critical to our national resilience as any component of national defense.

News can be overwhelming

I know the country seems fractured at the moment. And that the daily news headlines seem too much to bear. Some of you have told me you’re feeling overwhelmed by the challenges we face and uncertain about our ability to meet them.

But I would ask you to remember: Our shared values, our shared responsibility to one another and the country we all cherish – that’s been the hallmark of the American story for the past 20 years, for the past 245 years.

Even in these past 20 months, doctors, nurses, teachers, grocery clerks, truck drivers, people everywhere, have pulled together to keep our economy moving, our students learning and all of us healthy and safe.

We are a nation of more than 333 million people – of many colors and cultures, of many religions and political beliefs. But do you remember? We’re also a nation of Rosie the Riveters. Of Live Aid concerts and charity telethons, community bake sales and clothing drives. We’re the hearts and billfolds that open daily for the vulnerable among us – our elderly neighbors, the hungry, the homeless, victims of hurricanes and earthquakes.

That’s who we are. That’s in America’s DNA.

Common humanity unites us

We know that our humanity toward one another is our saving grace. We know this – not because we were always good to each other in the past, or because we’ve always been a truly United States.

We know it because, at times, we’ve strayed from that humanity, that empathy and that unity. We’ve learned from the consequences of our mistakes that America is not perfect – so we try harder and strive to be a more perfect union.

The late Sen. John McCain was a dear friend of mine for decades. “Do not despair of our present difficulties,” he said in his farewell message, “but believe always in the promise and greatness of America, because nothing is inevitable.”

John took nothing for granted. He fought every day of his life for the greater good. For the country he loved. For the cause he believed in most – service above self.

I’m profoundly grateful for the opportunities I was given to serve my country. From soldier to secretary, I’ve seen America on its worst days and its best. I’ve seen people give all they had to give. And I’ll never forget it.

I’ll never forget the silence on a Pennsylvania field one September morning.

Or the sacrifice of 40 heroes strong.

I’ll never forget all of those we lost 20 years ago. Too terribly and too soon.

May we keep their memories close – as well as each other.

Tom Ridge was governor of Pennsylvania on 9/11. He later served as the first U.S. secretary of Homeland Security.

search_result.title: Lower Manhattan seemed finished after 9/11. We knew better.
search_result.text:
Michael R. Bloomberg

Opinion contributor

Sept. 9, 2026, 5:06 a.m. ET

The attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, left wounds that time will never fully heal. Nearly 3,000 people were killed in a despicable act of terrorism – mothers and fathers, sons and daughters, family members and friends.

"Never Forget," we vowed together. But today, about 1 in 3 Americans are too young to remember 9/11. Part of our duty to those we lost, and to our country, is to teach them what happened that day and in the years after, so that they will pass the lessons on to their children and grandchildren.

The terrorists targeted New York City because it has long been a symbol of the freedoms they hated. They aimed not only to bring down buildings, but also to break our spirit and our commitment to the values that give us strength: openness, diversity, tolerance and ambition.

To see New York a quarter century later is to comprehend how profoundly they failed. The city is more vibrant, exciting and alive than ever before.

But 25 years ago, none of that was guaranteed.

Need a news break? Check out the all new PLAY hub with puzzles, games and more!

Lower Manhattan's long shadow

I was elected mayor less than two months after the attacks. A deep sense of uncertainty hung over the city’s future.

Many worried that Lower Manhattan would never recover – that no one would want to live or work in the area, and that as businesses and residents left, crime would return, infrastructure would crumble, and the city would slide back into the decline it had known in the 1970s.

All of us in elected office, in both parties, were determined not to let that happen. It would have handed the terrorists the victory they sought. We owed it to everyone we lost on 9/11 to prevent it.

I began my career in Lower Manhattan, just a few blocks from the World Trade Center, back when the area was the financial center of the city. It bustled during the day, but after 6 p.m. and on weekends, it became a ghost town of empty streets and closed shops. In 2001, it was still largely that way.

After 9/11, our team in City Hall believed that Lower Manhattan’s recovery depended not on rebuilding what had been lost, but on building something that had never fully existed there: a 24/7 community.

We set out to reimagine Lower Manhattan as a family-friendly neighborhood, one where more people would want to live, more entrepreneurs would want to open businesses, and more companies would want to operate: a "vibrant global hub of culture and commerce, a live-and-work-and-visit community for the world," as I described it back in 2002.

That vision led us to create new parks and open spaces, including along the city's long-neglected waterfront. It led us to build new schools to attract families and to make new investments in the arts. And it led us to form new partnerships with cultural organizations, including the inaugural Tribeca Film Festival in 2002, which helped show the world that Lower Manhattan was not just safe but also exciting, the place to be.

Ground Zero: Former World Trade Center location is a complicated site

As we worked to transform the neighborhood, however, Ground Zero remained empty. It was an extremely complicated site, controlled jointly by two states and a private developer, with many competing ideas and public debates about what should be done.

Despite good intentions, disputes led to delays that lasted years. By 2006, with progress on the memorial stalled, I agreed to step in to lead the effort – and vowed to open the memorial by the 10th anniversary of the attacks.

Working closely with state agencies, family members, construction companies, architects and others, we resolved thorny issues, got the project back on track and kept our promise. On Sept. 11, 2011, the 9/11 Memorial opened where the Twin Towers once stood. The name of each person we lost is etched in bronze around peaceful reflecting pools, with waterfalls that cascade beyond view.

Standing before it is a powerful experience more than 100 million people from around the world have now had. Many have also spent hours in the museum beneath it, learning about the day, the people we lost and the stories of heroism, sacrifice and compassion that inspired the world.

Revival of Lower Manhattan reflects New York City at its best

When we left City Hall at the end of 2013, life had already returned to the World Trade Center, and there were far more people living and working in Lower Manhattan than there had been on Sept. 10, 2001. That number has kept growing, as our vision for a 24/7 community continues to bear fruit.

In 2023, the Perelman Performing Arts Center (PAC NYC) opened beside the 9/11 Memorial and Freedom Tower. I was honored to chair the effort to build it, and it fulfilled the plan we had developed in City Hall for the arts to have a permanent home at the site.

People now go to the World Trade Center for the memorial, where they commemorate those we lost; for the museum, where they learn about 9/11; and for PAC NYC, where they take in world-class theater, dance and music. And they go to do what New Yorkers have always done: work, with tens of thousands of people now employed in the new towers.

Thanks to the hard work and cooperation of so many, the rebuilding of the World Trade Center and the revival of Lower Manhattan have led to the rebirth of a community that reflects New York City at its best: a place where people of all backgrounds and beliefs live, work, gather and play together, exercising the freedoms the terrorists could not destroy.

Lower Manhattan today stands as a testament to the strength and resilience of the city’s spirit – and our national character.

Michael R. Bloomberg, founder of Bloomberg and Bloomberg Philanthropies, is chair of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum and the Perelman Performing Arts Center (PAC NYC). He served as mayor of New York City from 2002 to 2013.

3:52 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update In Boston, pain remains, but 'hate cannot drive out hate' Bailey Allen Family members of Massachusetts residents killed in the Sept. 11 terror attacks gathered at the “Garden of Remembrance” in downtown Boston for a wreath-laying ceremony Friday afternoon. In attendance were Mayor Michelle Wu, Gov. Maura Healey, Lieutenant Gov. Kim Driscoll and U.S. Sen. Ed Markey. “It's really hard to grasp what 25 years means when it can feel like it's a such a long period of time and yet so fresh in our memories and still so, so painful,” Wu told the crowd. Patricia Cahill Hoban, who lost her brother John Cahill in the attacks, laid a wreath at the memorial with her husband, Bob. John Brett Cahill, 56, of Brookline, Massachusetts, was a passenger on United Airlines Flight 175, Hoban said. She said she thinks of her brother every day. And she said she has forgiveness in her heart for those who committed the attacks. “I forgave a long time ago,” Hoban said. “Hate cannot drive out hate.” Earlier in the day, a Sept. 11 memorial was held at Boston Logan International Airport, where American Airlines Flight 11 and United Airlines Flight 175 took off before being hijacked and flown into the World Trade Center in New York. Massachusetts Port Authority Chief Thomas Kinton spoke of the harrowing minutes, hours, days, and weeks after the attacks. “As I look around this morning, I see many people who were right beside me during that incredibly difficult time,” Kinton said. “People who picked us up from the tragedy and got to work.”

3:30 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update In Pennsylvania, 'faith and bravery can prevail' Madolin Edwards and Beth Ann Miller A gathering at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, came to a close with a laying of wreaths at the Wall of Names memorial. Earlier, Doug Burgum, secretary of the Department of the Interior, told the audience that it's not just remembering and honoring, "it's about action." Burgum said if it wasn't for the 40 people on Flight 93 who took action, "our world would be very different today. We can draw from their incredibly heroic actions." Gov. Josh Shapiro also spoke at the event, saying people in Pennsylvania carry a special responsibility to all those lost in 9/11 and "to all who bear the scars of that day." Gordon Felt, brother of Flight 93 passenger Edward P. Felt, said he felt the families of Flight 93 are forever in the debt of the community, who welcomed them and kept their stories alive. "For 35 minutes from the takeover until the plane went down, citizens fought the first battle in a long war," he said. "They won. The flag is still flying over the Capitol." Felt said Flight 93 did what the nation's founders would have recognized – making one out of many. "The unity was not in spite of their differences," he said. "It was made stronger by them." "Even in the shadow of death, faith and bravery can prevail," Felt added.

2:02 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update She was on Air Force One on 9/11. Here's what was happening in the air Irene Wright ATLANTA – Gathered inside the Buckhead Club, overlooking Atlanta's skyline to the south, members listened intently as Wanda Joell recounted her experience aboard Air Force One on Sept. 11, 2001. Joell, an Air Force veteran and the first African American flight attendant permanently assigned to the presidential plane, would serve under presidents George H.W. Bush, George W. Bush, Bill Clinton and Barack Obama over her four-decade career. But on this day 25 years ago, training went out the window when a plane flew into the World Trade Center. They were scheduled for a two-hour flight back to Washington, DC, from Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Sarasota, Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students. Joell was in the middle of her pre-flight duties when she went to place name cards in the flight's central conference room and noticed news alerts popping up on the plane's few television screens. "President Bush was determined to go back to Washington, the nation's capital. Of course, he was advised against it at the moment. He was coming out of his office, and we met in the hall and we had the chance to embrace," Joell said. "It was unexpected, but at the time it was everything. I felt the heaviness he was carrying." Joell said that moment was the highlight of her career, when she was able to "console a U.S. president." She described Bush as calm, and said that day taught her what leadership means.

12:56 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update 'Critically important' to remember those dead from 9/11-related health issues Miles J. Herszenhorn The 9/11 memorial ceremony at Ground Zero observed a new, seventh moment of silence to remember the thousands of first responders and civilians who have died from 9/11-related illnesses or injuries. The additional moment of silence took place after the conclusion of the reading of names of victims who died in the attacks. Gregory Carafello, a survivor of the attacks, said it is “critically important” to include an opportunity to remember the lives of those who died from working at Ground Zero. “A lot of them were volunteers,” Carafello said. “A lot of them were dump truck drivers and crane operators.”

12:55 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update Virginia Gov. Spanberger reflects on 9/11 unity, today’s division Karissa Waddick Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger said her 12-year-old daughter asked her this morning whether any of the plane passengers survived on 9/11. The question, Spanberger said, made her realize the next generation must be taught to “understand the devastation” of 9/11 and its lingering impacts. “That heaviness lasted,” she said, explaining that the response work begun that day still must continue. Reflecting on the country’s unity after 9/11, the governor said it was “a choice” people made.

12:36 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update Mourners remember passengers who overtook hijackers on Flight 93

12:30 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update 'Nobody knew what was going to happen next' Karissa Waddick Abandoned cars on thoroughfares. Bumper-to-bumper traffic. The uncanny silence. Firefighters running toward the smoke. At Arlington Firehouse 5, Virginia State Sen. Barbara Favalo remembered the chaos that unfolded around Washington, DC, in the hours after the Sept. 11 attacks. A firetruck from the station arrived at the Pentagon four minutes after the plane struck the building. The station served as the epicenter of the Pentagon response in the days and weeks after the attack. “It was something none of us had ever experienced before,” she said.

12:18 pm ET September 11, 2026 Share this update New Jersey ceremony aims to keep the 'promise we made on Sept. 11, 2001' Kyle Morel Hundreds of American flags lined the roads leading to Clifton City Hall, where residents and first responders gathered to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11.
