search_result.title: The 9/11 attacks hit 25 years ago. They're still shaping our lives
search_result.text:
Sept. 1, 2026 Updated Sept. 7, 2026, 4:01 p.m. ET

A quarter-century later, 9/11 still echoes.

The worst terrorist attack in U.S. history has been followed by other seismic events, from a once-in-a-century global pandemic to the rise of artificial intelligence that is transforming commerce, education and more. Nearly 100 million Americans − almost 1 in 4 − have no personal memory of the Sept. 11 attacks, born after it happened.

And yet.

The attacks continue to resonate in the lives of the families, friends and colleagues of the 2,977 victims who died and for the tens of thousands of survivors and first responders who are dealing with 9/11-related health issues.

In a spiderweb that has spread through the nation's laws, economy, warfare and culture, its repercussions are also felt by just about every American. Some of the questions it raised remain unsettled.

Consider: Extension of the post-9/11 law that allows warrantless surveillance abroad is stalled in a fierce congressional divide. The mistrust of officialdom about the attack and the war in Iraq that ensued helped lay the groundwork for current-day conspiracy theories about school shootings and election fraud. A new generation of video games inspired by 9/11 is being tapped as a controversial recruiting tool by the military and law enforcement in real life.

"We encounter an echo every time we go to an airport, obviously," with the creation of the Transportation Security Administration and tighter travel security regimes, said Mitch Daniels, a member of President George W. Bush's Cabinet who was on the White House campus when the planes struck the World Trade Center. Even amid the chaos of that moment, he recalled, "we knew something completely new and terrible had happened."

The consequences continue to reverberate. In some ways, Sept. 11 was 25 years ago, and also yesterday.

Here are three ways:

Where's the line? Liberty vs. security

In the immediate aftermath of 9/11, Americans were more than willing to trade liberty and privacy for a stronger sense of security.

Just weeks after the attacks, Congress passed the landmark USA Patriot Act by an overwhelming and bipartisan vote, expanding the government's investigative and surveillance powers. Later, the behemoth Homeland Security Department was created, and an overarching director of national intelligence position was installed.

By a double-digit margin in 2004, the public told a Pew Research Center poll that the anti-terrorism policies imposed so far had "not gone far enough to protect the country," rather than having "gone too far restricting civil liberties."

But about a decade later, there were second thoughts after abuses in surveillance were exposed by former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden in 2013. Then, by another double-digit margin, Americans said the anti-terror programs had gone too far.

Today, that debate has been joined again on Capitol Hill, where Congress has so far been unable to extend Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA). The law, which sunsetted in June, allows U.S. intelligence agencies to collect communications of foreign targets overseas without obtaining warrants, but in the process they have also incidentally swept up the phone calls, texts and emails of Americans.

Some warn that the hard lessons of 9/11 are being forgotten.

"You know, the dog that doesn't bite − it's easy to overlook," said Daniels, who after the attacks served two terms as governor of Indiana. His memoir, "Impatience is a Virtue," is being published by Lyons Press on Sept. 5. "Even though we may have strengthened ourselves against certain kinds of terrorism, we have opened ourselves up to others," including in the cyber world.

But in the House debate, Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky, called the existing law "an infringement of the Constitution."

Where do Americans now want to draw the line?

The road from '9/11 was an inside job' to election deniers

Conspiracy theories aren't new in America. Witness the Cold War speculation in the 1950s that adding fluoride to drinking water was, alternatively, a Communist plot or a CIA mind-control experiment. Or that the Apollo moon landing in 1969 was staged, the video shot on some clandestine movie set.

But the Sept. 11 attacks, which hit just as the internet was emerging as a force, accelerated a new era of conspiracy thinking that has moved from the political fringe to mainstream debate. With it, it has helped undermine faith that already was eroding in government, science and the news media.

"Around 9/11, a significant chunk of the public thought it was an inside job, who believed that the Bush administration either knew in advance or planned it as a pretext for Iraq," Matthew Baum, a professor at Harvard's Kennedy School whose studies include fake news and misinformation, said in an interview. "All the conspiratorial thinking that we have now been inundated with in the last decade in some ways traces back to that era."

The fact that weapons of mass destruction were never found in Iraq, the purported justification for the U.S. invasion, stoked the doubts.

Those who now follow QAnon or believe debunked conspiracies about the Sandy Hook school shooting form what scholars call a "through line" with the 9/11 doubters. These days, conspiracy theories range from the state of Kentucky Sen. Mitch McConnell's health to the real story behind sexual predator Jeffrey Epstein. (Even Vice President JD Vance declared in June, "I am frankly kind of a conspiracy theory on the Epstein stuff.")

While the number of people who believe in a conspiratorial world hasn't increased, there has been an impact on those who are no longer quite sure whether they can believe what experts and officials are saying. "A COVID false story, or an election false story − how many are willing to entertain that it might be true?" Baum asked. "Not hardcore conspiratorial people, [but] people who aren't confident enough to say, 'definitely not.'"

That nagging uncertainty creates an opening that can be exploited. For instance, more than 6 in 10 Republicans agree with Trump's discredited complaint that the 2020 election was stolen from him. The president now argues that the midterm elections are at risk of massive voter fraud.

Some Democrats fear Trump could use those unsubstantiated assertions as a pretext to intervene in November. In August, he refused to rule out declaring a national security emergency to impose new voting restrictions. "Stranger things have happened," he said.

Video warriors: It's not (just) a game

In the summer of 2001, the hottest gaming titles were video games like Pokémon Crystal (about fictional monsters) and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 (about skateboarding).

But in the wake of the attacks that September, a new generation of video games began to reflect the headlines. Terrorism and counterterrorism, intelligence ops and special forces, attacks on cities and public spaces moved to the center of gaming culture.

The blockbuster Call of Duty franchise, first released in 2003, is now the best-selling first-person shooter series ever. Decades later, scholars say the legacy of Sept. 11 continues to fuel the persistent demand for war-themed games.

"Post-9/11 shooters weaponized the shared sense of national trauma and powerlessness into profitable toys," said Matthew Payne, a professor at Notre Dame and author of "Playing War: Military Video Games After 9/11." Video games became one way those in the generation growing up in the shadow of Sept. 11 experienced and interpreted the attacks, experts say.

"These games clearly have political and ideological points of view," Payne told USA TODAY. "They typically represent U.S. military engagements and weapons of war in a positive light. The games present overly simplified worlds devoid of civilians, children, and animals, and there are no lasting consequences for players’ decisions. Enemies simply disappear from the battlefield following a level, and the player’s soldier never suffers from any mental or physical injuries."

Now the Pentagon and law enforcement agencies − and the White House − have mimicked video games in appeals targeting young people for recruitment.

In March, the White House posted a video on social media that mixed footage from Call of Duty with combat footage from U.S. strikes on Iran, set to a driving instrumental version of Childish Gambino's song "Bonfire." Another White House video, titled "UNDEFEATED," intercut footage of a Nintendo Wii game with real military attacks. The Department of Homeland Security and ICE, the immigration and customs agency, have borrowed from video games in their recruitment posters and social-media campaigns.

Veterans and religious leaders accuse the administration of trivializing warfare and its costs. "War is not a f------ video game," Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who lost both legs as a helicopter pilot in the Iraq War, protested in a social media post. Critics note that video games typically depict a world of moral clarity and clear-cut victories.

Though real life, and 9/11, have proved to be more complicated than that.

search_result.title: 9/11 25th anniversary events in NYC, Rockland and Westchester
search_result.text:
Updated Sept. 11, 2026, 7:01 p.m. ET

New Yorkers gathered to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11 at memorial sites across the state, sharing stories to honor those who died in connection to that fateful day and advocating for those still suffering from its aftershocks a generation later.

In the Lower Hudson Valley, local officials and community leaders were joined by hundreds at events in the villages, towns and cities across the region that is home to so many families, responders and survivors directly impacted by the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

Rockland County's 9/11 memorial ceremony was held Friday morning at the county's 9/11 memorial in Haverstraw Bay Park. Westchester County's 9/11 memorial ceremony was held in the afternoon at Kensico Dam Plaza in Valhalla.

How Rockland marked the 9/11 anniversary

At the Rockland ceremony, more than 300 people gathered Friday morning at the county's memorial site, including C. Scott Vanderhoef, who was Rockland County's Republican executive in 2001 and recalled that morning a quarter-century ago.

He was in his New City office when the first plane hit. Then the second plane struck, and they knew the nation was under attack. Soon, the 77-year-old said, “we recognized many Rocklanders, both fighting the fires and in the buildings, were lost, and we’ve been mourning for 25 years.”

Current Rockland County Executive Ed Day, a Republican, noted the losses on 9/11 in the county and the years after from 9/11 illnesses were “a painful reminder of the toll that did not end that day.”

Legislator Dana Stilley, a Democrat, spoke of how “we know in Rockland County [9/11] was never a distant tragedy,” as she stood in front of the county’s memorial that lists the names of county residents lost.

At 8:46 a.m., a bell tolled to mark when the first plane, American Airlines Flight 11, struck the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York City.

After a moment of silence, family members then read the names of those from Rockland who were lost, as a bell tolled for each name. The last name read was that of Robert Kirkpatrick, of Suffern, who was killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

Rockland County Sheriff Lou Falco said he remains humbled by the heroism responders displayed that day, noting he wanted to remember the 18 NYPD members who have died since that day who have been added to the Rockland County Police Memorial.

At 9:03 a.m., the bell tolled again to mark when the second plane, United Airlines Flight 175, struck the south tower of the World Trade Center in New York City.

Rockland resident Rita Harvey, accompanied by Neil Berg, then performed "Bridge Over Troubled Water," before Keith Rosario urged people to continue to tell the stories of 9/11 to those too young to remember when people were“choosing to stand up as everything is falling apart.”

Chaplain David Lothrop, who has led every Rockland 9/11 ceremony, said this may be his last. He said he had mourned with the families and told them he would always be there for them.

Gary Graifman, whose brother David Graifman died at the World Trade Center, led the crowd in singing “God Bless America.” And the service ended with ‘America the Beautiful’ sung by Jim Russell, of the sheriff's police division, before Rockland County Emerald Society played "Amazing Grace" as they retire the colors.

Portage County, Ohio, Sheriff Bruce Zuchowski, and his son, Brandon, a Garfield Heights, Ohio, firefighter, also attended Rockland County's 9/11 ceremony.

They planned later to go to Lower Manhattan to Ground Zero and view the September 11 Memorial.

Sheriff Zuchowski had recently discussed with other sheriffs from his state how he had hoped to visit New York and Ground Zero one day. They connected him with Rockland's Sheriff Falco.

"Just hearing the impact on the families," Bruce Zuchowski, 59, said, "was very moving." Brandon Zuchowski, 25, said he was honored to be able to mark the day with families of those who were lost. "It was a special to be a part of."

How Westchester remembered 9/11 on the 25th anniversary

At Westchester's Kensico Dam Plaza, the keening of bagpipes filled the air Friday afternoon. Then, a crowd listened as Sean Adams, Yonkers schools' press secretary, took them back 25 years to when he was a WCBS 880 radio reporter in Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001.

Adams, one of several speakers at Westchester County's Sept. 11 memorial, which the county government said was attended by about 560 people, was covering the Sept. 11, 2001, mayoral primary when he heard the station's traffic reporter in the helicopter reporting something happening.

"When I heard his words, it sent a chill down my spine, and I immediately headed downtown." Adams said, where he reported from the scene.

He found himself a block north of the World Trade Center complex. He was talking to someone from the mayor's press office. He had his back to the Twin Towers. He heard a noise, felt the ground shake, he said. He turned around.

"And then we ran for our lives," Adams said.

Adams said he and others got water "and we rinsed the eyes and the mouths of the dazed, dust-covered people who were coming out of that maelstrom."

He added: "We kept moving away. While we were doing that, even more first responders were coming in and they were rushing in."

Adams said he saw volunteers put together make-shift stretchers and organize blood donations in Foley Square. "With no regard for their own safety, first responders, they mounted that smoldering pile right away and they started digging their hands," he said.

Some responders refused to go home. They got a little rest in St. Paul's Chapel.

"And as they slept in the church where George Washington prayed after he was inaugurated," their boots scuffed some pews. "If you go to St. Paul's today, you can see those scuff marks — they've been left there."

For months and then years after, Adams said, families rallied to assist each other and organizations were formed to address the needs of families.

In time, illnesses from toxic exposure to the Ground Zero area claimed lives. The World Trade Center Health Program came to be.

"And thanks to that program and the brilliant scientists, doctors and nurses at Memorial Sloan Kettering right here in Westchester County, I am with you today," he said.

Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins, a Democrat, also addressed the community's commitment to keep telling 9/11 stories, saying at the ceremony that "25 years may have passed, but we have not forgotten."

"We have not forgotten those we lost," he said. "We've not forgotten our families, friends and loved ones who have carried that loss" to this day.

The service ended with family members and others reading the names of 123 Westchester County residents who died on 9/11 as well as names of some of the many others who died due to 9/11-related illness.

On Thursday, Westchester also held an interfaith vigil at the county's Sept. 11 memorial, the Rising. Among the speakers was the Rev. Kym McNair, Westchester County director of faith-based initiatives.

"You, who are the lifter of our heads and the healer of our hearts, we come pausing for just a moment in your time on this 25th observance of one of the most tragic days in this country's history," McNair said. "We come seeking the countenance of your glory shining through the memories of fear, terror and loss on that day. We come today as one body sharing the bonds of humanity."

Others who spoke at the interfaith vigil were Jenkins, Imam Shaffieq Chace of the Westchester Muslim Center, Lester Bronstein, rabbi emeritus of Bet Am Shalom Synagogue in White Plains, and Abhilash Tiwari of the Hindu Temple of Tri-State.

Inside the Sept. 11 ceremony in NYC

A ceremony commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks is taking place at Ground Zero in New York City.

Current and former dignitaries gathered at the 9/11 memorial in New York City, including Vice President JD Vance, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul.

Several former presidents were also in attendance, including Joe Biden, Barack Obama, George Bush and Bill Clinton.

Other officials at the ceremony include Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.

To watch the livestream, provided by USA TODAY, see the video below.

Nancy Cutler writes about People & Policy for lohud.com and the USA Today Network New York. Reach her at ncutler@lohud.com; follow her on Twitter, Threads and Instagram at @nancyrockland.
